Islamic State Conflict—Government Response

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I wish to make a ministerial statement. The
Government takes its national security obligations very seriously. As Prime Minister , I
have overarching responsibility for national security, and today I gave a speech on the
topic. I outlined how our risk and threat profile is changing, the challenges we face, and
how the Government is responding. Much of that  is due to the rapid rise of  the Islamic
State of Iraq and the Levant  (ISIL). Over the last 2 years it has seized substantial
territory in northern Iraq and Syria. New Zealanders will have seen the brutal and
distressing methods ISIL uses, including beheading displays and mass killin gs. ISIL’s
ability to motivate Islamic radicals, as well as its growth ambitions, resources, and
methods, make it a brutal threat to stability not only in the Middle East but regionally
and locally too. It is estimated ISIL has around 12,000 to 15,000 fore ign terrorist
fighters, of whom as many as 3,000 hold Western passports from a range of countries.
The rise of such a well -resourced, globally focused terrorist entity, highly skilled in
recruitment techniques using social media, is a game-changer for New  Zealand. ISIL
exposes us to a type of threat that we lack the legislative tools and resources to combat.
As in other Western countries, ISIL has been successful in recruiting New Zealanders to
the cause. Government agencies have a watch-list of between 30  and 40 people of
concern in the foreign fighter context. These are people in or from New Zealand who
are in various ways participating in extremist behavi our. Some of those on the watch -
list have travelled to Syria to engage in fighting, and remain there.  Others are ISIL
supporters who have tried to travel to Syria or to Iraq to fight and have been prevented
from leaving by cancellation of their passports.
Although I am limited in what I can say, it is important to note there are individuals
here in New Zealand who are attracted to carrying out domestic attacks of the type that
we have seen prevented in Australia and that took place in Canada. I want to stress that
none of these people is a representative of the New Zealand Muslim community, and I
know tha t the vast majority of Muslims here are as distressed by ISIL’s actions and
violent message as anybody is. As a Government, we are doing what we can to prevent
New Zealanders from going off to fight for ISIL and brutally killing innocent civilians
in Iraq and Syria. Should they return to New Zealand fully radicalised and skilled in
fighting, they will represent a significant threat to the safety of New Zealanders , so we
have been cancelling people’s passports where necessary. But even those radicalised
New Zealanders who have been prevented from travelling are a threat to our safety and
security. In addition to those on the watch-list, there are another 30 to 40 people on a list
of people requiring further investigation. These people c ould well be added to t he
watch-list or given the all-clear. We will not know that until those investigations can be
properly carried out.
I announced today that Cabinet has agreed to a proposal for law changes in the short
term—ones that cannot wait for the broader intelligenc e review required by law next
year. I intend to seek broad political support to pass this very limited legislation, which I
trust that other parties will see as narrow and responsible . The first change is to give the
Minister of Internal Affairs the abilit y to cancel a passport on the grounds of national
security for to up to 3 years. At the moment the Minister can do that for only up to 1
610 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
year. Secondly, I intend to allow the Minister to suspend a passport or travel document
for a temporary period of no mo re than 10 working days. This would be used where
urgent action is required but time is not available to prepare a full package of
information to support a cancellation. Thirdly , the S IS will be given a $7 million
funding injection across the current and n ext financial year s to increase the number of
staff it has to monitor and investigate foreign terrorist fighters.
Finally, I want to update one aspect of the S IS surveillance powers. The S IS cannot
generally undertake visual surveillance in a private sett ing, or which would involve
trespass on to private property. This means, for example, that the service cannot install a
video camera in private premise s even if it was to observe activities of a security
concern, like people training with weapons. This iss ue was dealt with on the police’s
behalf in the Search and Surveillance Act of 2012. I am proposing that the S IS be given
the power under warrant and with additional safeguards modelled on the Search and
Surveillance Act. I am also proposing that the SIS be given an emergency surveillance
power for a period not exceeding 48 hours to conduct surveillance before a warrant can
be issued.
The second aspect of our response to ISIL relates to our contribution to the
international coalition fighting this entity. To manage a threat like this we need to be
well informed and share information with our partners, which is the role of the
intelligence agencies. We will be stepping up our contribution to intelligence operations
that offer opportunities to further understand and potentially disrupt ISIL. We will a lso
be building capability to monitor threats from any offshoots of ISIL that threaten us at
home.
ISIL is not a short -term threat. Defeating it will mean winning the hearts and minds
of those vulnerable to its destructive message. New Zealand , as a good international
citizen and as a country now elected to serve on the U nited Nations Security Council,
needs to play its part in ensuring that the longstanding and, some would say, intractable
problems of the Middle East are addressed. Over the nex t 2 years we have the
opportunity to attempt to ensure that the council, designed to address these major issues
of stability and security, lifts its game.
The situation in Syria and Iraq is an extreme humanitarian emergency with millions
displaced by conflict. New Zealand has provided $13.5 million in aid to the region since
the start of the Syrian crisis in 2011, and I am pleased to announce a further $1 million
contribution today to help refugees and the internally displaced. We will also be looking
at further assistance to meet the needs of Syrian and Iraqi refugees.
Moving on to assisting in building a disciplined and efficient military in Iraq, New
Zealand cannot, and should not, fight Iraqis’ battles for them. In the speech today I
ruled out sending SAS or any troops into combat roles in Iraq. Our military can and may
well play a part in building the capability and capacity of the Iraqi forces. Should
military personnel be deployed in Iraq they would be behind the wire and limited to
training local fo rces in order to counter ISIL and legitimately protect innocent people.
Cabinet has asked for further advice on this training option, which will be filled by
regular forces. That advice will take some time to b e completed and will involve
assessing how saf e and secure a training location is and whether our security
requirements can be met. We are talking to our longstanding partner Australia about
what it is  doing to help train the Iraqi forces and how we might help. New Zealand
military planners will trave l to the Middle East to assess the training option, and then
provide further information to Cabinet.
We are also looking at where our military could make a contribution outside Iraq by
supporting more longstanding operations where our partners have reloca ted resources to
address ISIL. All of this will be carefully thought through before final decisions are
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 611
made. As I said in the speech today, New Zealand has long been portrayed as having a
benign threat environment. It gives me no pleasure to say that this  is changing. New
Zealanders can be sure that we are taking careful and responsible steps to protect their
safety and security.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: First of all, I would
like to thank the Prime Minister for the opportunity for the House to respond to his
ministerial statement. It is at times like this that Parliament can be at its best. It is a time
when politicians can show New Zealanders that reas oned and constructive debate is
possible on issues of national and international importance.
The speech given by the Prime Minister this morning and the statement we have just
heard in the House today regarding his Government’s legislative response, aid, and
diplomatic efforts to combat the atrocities occurring in Iraq and Syria by the Islamic
State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) warrant our serious consideration and full debate. Security
at home and protection of New Zealand citizens must always be a top priori ty for any
Government—security on our streets, security in our homes, in our workplaces, in our
schools, and so on. New Zealanders expect Governments to take necessary measures to
protect them and their families from preventable danger, within the bounds o f reason
and within our obligations under international and domestic law —human rights law,
international refugee law, and international humanitarian law.
New Zealand does have a proud record in upholding fundamental freedoms and the
rule of law. We have, as a country, managed to balance the need for security and respect
for human rights. At times it can be difficult to have that balance. Hindsight is often
used to look at the decisions made after the event. Today, people are expecting
Parliament to get the  balance right—to arrive at a response to the growing unrest and
violence by ISIS in a calm and proportionate way.
The legislation that has been outlined by the Prime Minister today seeks to extend
the powers of the SIS to investigate and monitor people w ho may be a threat to our
security. Our role as the Opposition is to question the balance and to be vigilant in terms
of the legislation on behalf of New Zealanders. The provisions in the legislation are to
be parallel to those currently available to the p olice under the Search and Surveillance
Act, which would enable visual surveillance in private places. The powers of the SIS are
also to be extended to authorise surveillance activities to be undertaken in an emergency
situation, without warrant, for the duration of no more than 48 hours.
There must be safeguards, Prime Minister, to prevent abuse, and appropriate
warrants should be issued as quickly as possible in these very rare circumstances. We
would not want to see the 48 hours become the minimum or th e standard operating
procedure, which we have actually seen from the Government, in terms of Official
Information Act requests, waiting until the legal time is up before releasing information.

items.speaker: So we are saying
items.text: “Do not let the 48 hours become the norm.” If  it can be done faster, it
ought to be done faster. If the Prime Minister is not available within 48 hours to approve
the warrant, then there should be an alternative available.
We will examine the provisions very carefully at the select committee to ensu re
safeguards are in place to minimise potential abuse of the extended power. We will also
require that, when reporting on the number of warrants issued under this provision, the
Prime Minister report on how long it took before approval was given. I think that will
give us a pretty good idea of how fast warrants like this can be regularised. The
legislation also provides powers to disrupt and restrict travel by those seeking to fight
alongside designated terrorist groups. The right to free travel by New Zea landers is a
precious one, and we are keen international travellers. But clearly there are grounds
where restrictions can be justified. A person intent on engaging in terrorist acts or
612 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
seeking to join with organisations that are committing crimes against h umanity are such
grounds.
The United Nations Security Council in Resolution 2178 on 24 September this year
expressed grave concern about the acute and growing threat posed by foreign terrorist
fighters, those who attempt to travel to become foreign terror ist fighters, and the
recruitment of foreign terrorist fighters. As a member of the United Nations Security
Council and as good international members, New Zealand needs to heed those grave
concerns and put in place appropriate measures. However, the cancel lation of a passport
while a New Zealander is overseas cannot be undertaken lightly. It will be important
that any New Zealand citizen, when this happens, is issued with travel documents so
that they can return to New Zealand immediately. It would not make  sense to render a
person stateless and increase their potential to re-engage with a terrorist group.
Labour broadly supports the provisions as outlined today, and we believe that they
appear to be justified to ensure safety at home as well as meeting our  international
obligations. As I said, our role ought to be vigilant, to closely examine the bill at the
select committee, and to ensure the measures are workable, are necessary, and are
framed appropriately. We are glad that it is going to the select comm ittee to enable New
Zealanders to have a say. I thought, at one stage, that there was some doubt that that
might happen, but I am pleased that it is going to a select committee, even if the process
is truncated. The Australians managed to send their legisl ation to the Senate and to the
Lower House.
After what has felt like decisions made on the drip-feed—a snippet here, a clue there,
and a hint dropped over there —we are finally seeing the Government’s contribution to
the conflict caused by ISIS. The Minist er of Foreign Affairs has announced
humanitarian support for refugees from Syria and Iraq, and has ramped up diplomatic
efforts to address the rise of ISIS. We support such measures. It is clear to us that New
Zealanders support an approach like this rathe r than front -line troops, or even SAS
troops fighting on the front line.
If, Prime Minister, the next step by the Government is to involve New Zealanders in
some sort of military involvement, we think it is also clear that the majority of New
Zealanders would like such a decision to be backed by the United Nations. We urge the
Government to use the mandate it now has, as a member of the Security Council, to
speak up on behalf of a mandated approach to those countries, to use the influence that
we have over the next 2 years.
Bill English was the leader of the National Party in 2003 when Labour decided not to
go into the war in Iraq. At that time he said he wanted openness and honesty. That is
what he got then and that is what this Parliament is asking for n ow. Nobody wants to
see the spread of war or the atrocities that have been perpetrated on innocent people, not
least the people who live in those countries or the families who are in New Zealand.
Christopher Finlayson and I recently met with some of those families who are so fearful
for what is happening to their families in those countries. What we can do, in terms of
helping refugees fleeing from those countries, is to back and support them.
Can I conclude by saying that I have always liked the quotes of  Mahatma Gandhi,
and this is one I think is appropriate today. He said: “An eye for an eye makes the world
blind.” Thank you.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā kouto u e te
Whare. The Green Party stands for peace and for freedom. Peace is the best weapon that
we have in achieving personal security. It is a simple fact that New Zealanders are safest
in a peaceful world. Our democracy is only as strong as our personal fr eedoms. When
personal freedoms are eroded, our democracy is weakened.
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 613
Today John Key has eroded our quest for peace both at home and abroad, and has
eroded New Zealanders’ personal freedoms. By offering support to the US -led war with
the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), he leads us into part of a strategy that reduces
the prospects of enduring peace in the Middle East, and in the process we are also being
told we have to give up freedoms here at home. That is a lose-lose strategy.
We believe that r educed international and national security, the erosion of civil
liberties in New Zealand, and the introduction of the politics of fear into our national
debate is much too high a price to pay for involvement in the US -led efforts against
ISIS. The Green P arty stands for an entirely different approach. We believe there is a
better alternative. Rather than yet again pursuing the tried and failed approach of
military incursion into the Middle East, resulting in increased radicalism and surges in
terrorist activity, we should instead lead efforts that result in genuine peace and security.
This is the test that we would apply to our Government’s actions. Does our course of
action lead to peace abroad and greater security at home, and does our course of action
strengthen or weaken personal liberties? It is our view that the approach set out by John
Key today takes us further from peace and weakens our democracy. We stand for peace
overseas that delivers freedom at home.
New Zealand has a rightfully proud record o f trying to do the right thing in the
world. The value of our independent and principled foreign policy was recently
highlighted by the trust placed in us by those countries that supported us in the United
Nations Security Council bid. When needed and when  right, we have not been afraid to
roll up our sleeves and work with others to achieve lasting peace in the world.
Sometimes this has meant dying alongside other countries. But ever since the war in
Viet Nam we have learnt to question our involvement in th e wars that our traditional
allies have entered into around the globe. We have been better off for this questioning
approach. The 10 -year war that followed the US invasion of Iraq in 2003 we wisely
stayed out of. It was the right thing to do. That war ende d inconclusively, at great cost
to both the US and Iraq, and played a big part, perversely, in the rise of ISIS.
Supporting war, whether directly with boots on the ground or through other actions,
is one of the most important decisions that we as a nation  can ever make. It is our view
that through our intelligence -gathering activities and support for US -led efforts New
Zealand is part of the American war effort. What John Key has set out is New Zealand’s
clear support for those fighting the war with ISIS.
Today the Green Party is clear in its position. We do not support any form of military
engagement with the war effort. This includes training support for the Iraqi army.
Regardless of how the Government seeks to frame it, the reality is that any military
assistance is a contribution to the war effort. It is our view that the war effort will not
result in peace. It is a strategy without an end point and has a low chance of success. It
is a myth that Western intervention can destroy ISIS. A war will not solv e what is, at
heart, sectarianism in Iraq.
Ten years of war waged by America could not solve the tensions that divide Sunni
and Shi’a Iraqis or divide extremists from the moderates, so how will this time be any
different? Even an intensive, decades -long American ground effort, something that is
politically not on the table, might only make the problem worse. ISIS’s presence in Iraq
and Syria is fundamentally a political problem, not a military one. Doug Ollivant,
national security adviser for Iraq from 2005 to 2009, told Vox Media: “I take the
somewhat modest position that the actions of 6 million Iraqis may be more important
than those of 30,000 troops and one very talented general,”.
The world can defeat ISIS and build a lasting peace. We in the Greens are committed
to this outcome, but there are better ways to achieve it. There are better ways to achieve
it than through military Western intervention.
614 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
The Green Party strongly supports a commitment to additional humanitarian aid in
the region and a commitment to finding an enduring political soluti on to the war in the
Middle East, especially now that we are in the key position to do so, on the Security
Council. By contributing humanitarian aid, New Zealand can demonstrate that our
primary concern is for the needs of the victims, particularly childre n. By contributing
our independent foreign diplomacy at the UN, New Zealand can demonstrate our
commitment to collective peace and security, the only real long -term solution to the
horror of war and terrorism. If New Zealand wants to make a difference on t he Security
Council, by going in clean we will be more credible advocates for finding a political
solution in the Middle East.
Any military deployment in the Middle East will undermine our peace and security
here at home. Although this is not a compelling  reason on its own to avoid engaging in
conflicts around the world where it is just and the outcome will be lasting, this US -led
war against ISIS does not justify those costs that we will bear here at home.
Rather than eroding our civil liberties, it is n ow time to strengthen our tolerant and
free democratic society. Rather than shutting down, it is now time to open up. Let us
look at what enlightened leaders are doing to reduce the risk posed by foreign fighters,
rather than rely on the failed policies of the Abbott Government in Australia. Joining the
US-led war in the Middle East is already increasing the climate of fear back here at
home. We saw it in the Prime Minister’s speech today and in his recent statements. Fear
pervades the drip -feeding of alleg ations that raise suspicions about our neighbours and
others who share our community. Fear is the tried and true playbook of those who seek
to build artificial walls between us.
The Green Party rejects becoming a nation of fear. Fear is the breeding ground for
intolerance, violence, and the slow, sure erosion of our own hard -fought-for rights,
freedoms, and duties to one another.
Today John Key announced the erosion of a few more of our rights as citizens. There
will be $7 million of funding for our secret services, increased scope for the State to
cancel New Zealanders’ passports, and, most problematically, the expansion of video
surveillance by the SIS without the prior need for  a warrant. The continual
encroachment of the surveillance State here in our home is part and parcel of the
commitment to the war on terror abroad. War abroad and spying here at home are two
sides of the same coin. Our police already have extensive and suf ficient powers to pre -
empt an investigation into crime that is being planned here in Aotearoa New Zealand.
We have no clear evidence for more. We will not stand by and watch New Zealand
become another paranoid society —one where our secret services have eve n greater
powers to spy on us, one where our freedoms are progressively withdrawn, and one
where spending on security becomes a higher priority than the crisis of New Zealand’s
child poverty.
Today I speak on behalf of a truly independent foreign policy that works for peace as
the best form of security —a foreign policy that aligns foreign and domestic interests. I
speak on behalf of our personal freedoms. I put them on a pedestal, to be eroded only in
the most extreme of cases. I speak on behalf of those N ew Zealanders who believe in
alternatives to war and fear and those who aspire to genuine peace and freedom. Thank
you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: New Zealand Fir st welcomes
the chance to debate the Prime Minister’s statement today on the Government’s
response to the threat of the Islamic State movement and the proposed new legislative
powers to counter the threat of international terrorism. We share the view that the threat
posed by the Islamic State is indeed very serious and there are no grounds for
complacency.
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 615
Welcome as it is, we do consider the Prime Minister’s statement to be seriously
overdue and lacking chronological detail. There has been enough delay. T here has been
far too much prevarication. New Zealanders have seen events unfolding internationally
and have had only a vague and indefinite comment from time to time from the Prime
Minister. In the area of national security, the public must take so much o n trust alone.
That is because, understandably, nearly all the work has to be done behind closed doors,
but a Government has a duty to keep the public as informed as it can be on what
commitments and undertakings are being given in the area of internationa l security.
Ultimately, it is the public who will pay the price of those commitments.
In our view, up until now the Prime Minister has been less than forthright. We do
note that the briefings given to journalists such as David Fisher in today’s New Zealand
Herald on page A15 are far more substantial than the briefings that were given to us.
Why that would be the case and we should be expected to go along with the
Government is beyond us, but there it is. That briefing is more comprehensive, I
believe, than that given to other parliamentary parties.
The result has been that the public’s confidence that the Prime Minister will act with
the highest integrity in relation to security issues has been eroded. But today the Prime
Minister has finally set out his Government’s response in terms of changes to strengthen
anti-terrorism legislation and how New Zealand can contribute to the wider
international effort to combat the Islamic State.
At this juncture it is important that New Zealanders know where New Zealand First
stands on these important issues. The changing context is important. New Zealand
enjoys a great geographical advantage in our distance from the world’s troubled regions.
To an extent, that the distance is, in an era of global terror threats, an illus ion. But what
is evident is that we are part of the global community. Events in the Middle East matter
to New Zealand. The Islamic State movement is a deeply disturbing development that
has unleashed a form of barbarism that no responsible country can ignore.
On the issue of New Zealand’s national security matters, New Zealand First stands
with some basic principles. First, our national security is ultimately our most important
national interest. The first duty of any Government is to ensure the safety and  protection
of its citizens. New Zealand First has always taken the view that this is the primary
responsibility of the Government but, equally, that Opposition parties must also display
responsibility. Second, New Zealand has a great stake in a stable international order. We
are a small and essentially defenceless nation. The last thing we want is international
disorder and chaos. Third, New Zealand’s capacity to contribute to international efforts
against terrorism is small. We must make careful and consi dered decisions. There is
nothing to be gained from pretending otherwise.
But this is a time when we can reflect on what Edmund Burke, the great British
political thinker, observed: “Nobody made a greater mistake than he who did nothing
because he could do only a little.” Accordingly, we do support some of the measures the
Prime Minister has mentioned today as ways New Zealand can contribute to the
international effort against the Islamic State, such as intelligence cooperation and
diplomatic and humanitarian support. On the issue of audio -surveillance, if the laws are
transposed from audio surveillance to visual surveillance, then they cannot really be an
expansion—it is just an inclusion of better technology.
But the Prime Minister must be clear and uneq uivocal on the issue of committing
New Zealand to a combat role. Any New Zealand military forces sent to the Middle
East will be construed by the Islamic State as in effect combat -related. Yesterday the
Prime Minister denied Cabinet had made a decision. Th at denial was patently false. The
people who briefed us had already told us that Cabinet had made a decision, so why the
Prime Minister rose in the House yesterday and denied it is beyond me. Second, as
616 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
those denials were being sounded there were military planners who had already left
New Zealand to act on behalf of this country, suggesting that a Cabinet decision had
already been made.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Already there.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Well, if they are alr eady there, why was there the
denial in the House yesterday on such a serious matter? Cooperation with Australia is
also going to be construed by the Middle East in the same way as we would construe it
if we were being neutral.
We cannot slip into combat by stealth. We cannot support policy when we are not
being told the full truth, open and honestly, on the related issue of strengthening some
legislation in the areas of passport controls and, as I said, visual surveillance and
providing extra funding for the SIS. We will need to see the full details before reaching
a final position. But in our view it is right that the Government should seek as wide a
degree of cross -party support as possible for national security issues and matters. That
means taking other parties into its confidence and not giving preference to journalists in
terms of information, as is so clearly demonstrated in evidence on page A15 of the New
Zealand Herald today.
We will consider the proposed legislative package carefully and responsi bly. Our
evaluation will be informed by the principle that on questions of national security New
Zealand First takes a realistic stance. We live in the real world, and in this regard we are
highly critical of the Government’s open -door immigration policy. If people over there
are so concerned about this matter, then why has there been such a loose immigration
policy for so long? Who is here who should not be here? What checks have been made?
We are not satisfied that the level of scrutiny and checking that immigrants are given is
adequate, given the nature of modern terrorism. We cannot put our heads in the sand in
a world of extremists and terrorists such as the Islamic State that stand opposed to
everything we value as a democratic and free society.
To ignore the threat posed by the Islamic State would be irresponsible, and recent
events graphically illustrate that terrorism can now be home grown and it also does not
respect international borders. Yet New Zealanders enjoy civil liberties that must not be
abandoned lightly or casually in a rush to be seen to be doing something.
Coming back to the point, if we are going to carry on with our open -door
immigration policy with so little scrutiny, then there cannot be people over there who
are seriously being gen uine in their concerns. For this reason New Zealand First will
assist the Government to meet legitimate national security goals as long as we are
satisfied that the extra legislation, as outlined by the Prime Minister today, is fully
needed and justified. On national security or on any other issue New Zealand First will
not be rubber-stamping legislation.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr
Speaker. Kia ora tātou katoa e te Whare. I stand to follow on from other speakers in
respect of the opportunity given by the Prime Minister to make a statement today.
Today’s announcement about the possibility of New Zealand entering into a war
against the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria is set against, in some senses, some uncanny
circumstances. Today Māoridom, at least, and those of Taranaki think about the cost
and the casualties of Parihaka, and also, of course, tonight is an acknowledgment of the
works of Mr Guy Fawkes, a ritual that has no cultural relevance to Aotearoa.
It was 133 years ago, early in the morning of 5 November 1881, that a small New
Zealand settlement was the scene of one of the worst infringements of civil and human
rights ever committed and witnessed in this country. A gentle rural community was
invaded by 150 militia and armed members of the constabulary. As innocent children
welcomed the army w ithin their midst, over 2,000 locals watched on in silence. This
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 617
was not an invasion by foreign troops on our own soil. Amongst the military forces in
attack were politicians, driven by their hunger for the rich, fertile, prime lands of
Taranaki. The force s were led, in fact, by two members of Parliament, both Cabinet
Ministers.
In respect of Mr Guy Fawkes, it is my suggestion that today, although there might be
sparklers and rockets throughout the country tonight, most New Zealanders will not be
aware of the history that comes from that event—namely, a plot to blow up Westminster
Palace and to take the life of the then monarch, King James I.
I pay particular reference to Parihaka on this historical day because it provides a
glimpse into war in our own nat ion. It gives some sense of harm caused to generations
of families through the military action. The people of Parihaka commonly refer to that
as Te Pāhuatanga o Parihaka, the invasion of Parihaka. It is still even today spoken
about.
The Māori Party is strongly opposed to New Zealand taking up military involvement
in Iraq in a civil war not of our making. During the 2003 to 2013 deployment in
Afghanistan, Aotearoa lost 10 New Zealand soldiers. As a nation we suffered the loss of
lives through military presence in Afghanistan, at a great and enduring cost to the well -
being of families and communities living here.
There is another reason why I wanted to refer to Parihaka. Parihaka was also the
birthplace, of course, of the unique movement of passive resistan ce associated with the
visionary leadership of Te Whiti o Rongomai and Tohu Kākahi. Both men were
committed to non -violent action, drawing on ancestral wisdom to offer both spiritual
and political leadership while war broke out all around them.
There are other options that we could explore. We welcome the emphasis that the
Prime Minister gave in his statement today towards humanitarian aid. The expression of
manaakitanga in a global context is demonstrated by the commitment to increased
support for refugee s from Syria and Iraq who have fled their homes in terror as the
result of the ongoing violence. This is a responsibility for peacemaking at an
international level, which we absolutely support. It is a responsibility that is consistent
with other members w ho have held my office, such as Sir Apirana Ngata, who soon
after war was announced in 1939 put into words the sacrifice our whānau were prepared
to make. He said: “We are participants in a great Commonwealth, to the defence of
which we cannot hesitate to contribute our blood and our lives. … We are of one house,
and if our Pakeha brothers fall, we fall with them. How can we ever hold up our heads,
when the struggle is over, to the question: ‘Where were you when New Zealand was at
war?’ ”.
Our participation  in serving the nation in such a way came as a result of our
commitment to honouring the obligations and duties, which we believe came out of the
covenant we signed in the Treaty of Waitangi, Te Tiriti o Waitangi. We commend that
generosity of spirit, that  incredible sacrifice of life and limb, that has caused enduring
harm to the spirit of the generations who follow.
I want to take us back to the last decade of deployment to Afghanistan. Those 10
fallen soldiers, killed in attacks in the Bamian Province, or Kabul, were aged between
21 and 41. Seven were in their 20s —young New Zealanders starting off in life, their
lives brutally cut short. We cannot forget their sacrifice, and indeed the sacrifices of the
Second World War, of the Korean War, of the Malayan emergency, and so on. The New
Zealand Army, Ngāti Tūmatauenga, has served with distinction in the major conflicts in
the 20 th century; it has given so much to fight for, for the honour of our country
overseas. But when do we get around to having the natio nal discussion around military
contribution?
618 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
Although the statement today —thankfully—rules out sending the SAS, or any other
troops, into the combat roles in Iraq, it does state that the military can, and may well,
help with building the capacity and capability of Iraqi forces. It also indicates a
willingness to help train the Iraqi forces, to deploy military planners to the Middle East
to determine whether New Zealand can play a role in helping Iraqi defence forces. We
understand the importance of diplomatic and intelligence measures in order to enga ge,
but the Māori Party asks: “What makes the training work any different to being in the
front line, firing the guns?”. Although there is a clear statement that there will be no
combat role in Iraq, we are not convinced that helping to train the Iraqi for ces is
sufficiently removed from the combat zones.
Throughout the wars of the 1860s the Parihaka leaders forbade the use of arms and
condemned violence and greed, and in doing so they modelled the art of passive
resistance as a template for healing a nati on, for responding to conflict through
peacemaking and dialogue. We have a proud history of protecting communities through
different means, through peace building. This is an opportunity, we say, surely to ensure
that our distinctive legacy of peaceful action might be useful.
There is one other area that I want to touch on and that is the increased authority and
intervention by the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service to carry out video
surveillance on private properties for the purpose of observing a ctivities. The Māori
Party will stand on record as stating our absolute opposition to any such actions that
would see a repeat of Operation Eight, in which the innocent lives of the whole
communities of Ruātoki were trampled on, traumatised, and for ever c hanged as a result
of the heavy hand of the State.
We stand alongside the Tūhoe nation, who have only just received the formal
acknowledgment by the Crown  in the last few months, or at least by the police as well,
of those injuries that occurred on 15 Oct ober 2007. This incident was disproportionate
surveillance under the guise of national security. What the Independent Police Conduct
Authority has concluded is that the police failed to meet expected standards when
carrying out the Ruātoki and Tāneatua road blocks and five of the 41 property searches.
Tūhoe, Ruātoki, Tāneatua—let us not forget that we have raised these concerns at the
highest levels and we expect this action to never occur again.
We do support the need for citizens in their areas to have t he ability to look after
themselves, to be self -determining, and to be able to care for themselves against the
atrocities of war, but we will never ever support any contribution of a military nature
that seeks to strengthen the potency of Iraqi forces to fight others. Our focus will always
be on being a good international citizen, promoting models of peace, and supporting the
well-being of families to care for themselves, but we can do that in a peacemaking and
humanitarian mode, not in the context of civil  war. We have a great international
reputation of providing humanitarian support. Let us stay where we are strong. N ō reira,
kia ora tātou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I welcome the opportunity to
take part in this debate this afternoon in response to the Prime Minister’s statement on
the Government’s response to the Islamic State conflict. I think it is a good step for this
House to be following. But I think the next  step is for such statements in future to be
made directly to Parliament and not to an interested audience of notables and worthies
outside Parliament in advance of this important occasion.
From the time of the Balfour Declaration in 1917 through to the m ost recent
American intervention in Iraq, the history of Western intervention in the Middle East
has not always led to peaceable outcomes. We have certainly seen more confusion,
more upheaval, and more bitterness created by some of those interventions over  the
years, and that is why I think the Government has taken a prudent course in ruling out
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 619
any form of military involvement by New Zealand in the campaign against Islamic State
of Iraq and Syria (ISIS). I think that that is not just recognition of our par ticular
strength, or lack thereof, but it is also correct in terms of the course of history, and I
must say in passing that the sending of military advisers to Iraq is, in my view, at the
outer limit of acceptability.
But the issue really now comes down t o a humanitarian one. No one, anywhere, can
tolerate the barbarity, the brutality, the exhibitionism, and the crudity of the ISIS
terrorists. What we have seen in the media and social media is unacceptable by any
norm, but we need to be very careful that w e do not transfer our abhorrence of this
behaviour into a lack of understanding, or a preparedness to even consider, the political
views that lie behind that most brutal expression. That is why it is appropriate for
countries like New Zealand to work throu gh humanitarian assistance to the affected
parties and, as the Prime Minister’s speech earlier today made reference, to assist with
the construction of sound institutions of State and forms of governance to promote
democratic ideals—to promote the sorts of values that we might regard as important in a
free society —rather than a brutal suppression of those ideas because we abhor the
methods that the proponents use. Just as we might later today celebrate —although some
of us might commiserate with—the demise of Guy Fawkes 500 years ago because of the
methods that he used, we cannot get into the same risk with regard to our treatment of
the ISIS terrorists.
There are a number of measures contained in the Prime Minister’s announcement
that I want to comment on specifically. If I can put on my hat as the Minister of Internal
Affairs for just a moment, I think that the changes proposed to the passports legislation
are appropriate. The current legislation has been shown to have some deficiencies,
particularly in ter ms of the duration of a suspension, but also in the definition used,
which at the moment is specific to the interests of New Zealand. The question that then
arises is how those interests might be interpreted. Are they New Zealand’s domestic
interests or wi der interests, or a combination of both? So I think that the changes
proposed in that respect are positive, and there are safeguards contained within those
proposals that mean that we will not get a ridiculous or rampant use of those provisions.
I think t he same can be said for the changes regarding surveillance by the SIS,
although I have some misgivings about aspects of that, but, broadly speaking, they line
up with the provisions that the police already have. They will be subject to a warrant,
and that warrant, under the legislation changes last year, is much more accountable
publicly than was the case previously. In an ideal world these changes would have
awaited the outcome of the review of the SIS and the Government Communications
Security Bureau due to occur after 30 June next year, but I accept that that may not be a
practical step, even though it might be a preferable one, and I think that the idea of
therefore having some sunset clauses about those particular provisions is a good one.
But I echo a comment that was made by an earlier speaker. I want to ensure that the
sunset clause is exercised not at the last minute, but as soon as the changes that arise
from the review next year are put in place.
I must say that I do have some concerns about the a dditional funding of $7 million
being advanced to the SIS. I think that that is a matter that requires more scrutiny in
terms of the direction of that expenditure —the purposes to which it is being put —and I
am sure that that is something the Intelligence a nd Security Committee will turn its
mind to in due course. Beyond that, there was a comment in the Prime Minister’s
statement regarding greater international intelligence cooperation. I have some very real
misgivings about that because I have lingering con cerns about the capacity of our
Government Communications Security Bureau to contribute effectively to that process.
It seems to me that what we are reliant on in a lot of cases is external intelligence
620 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
coming into New Zealand to assist us in the decisions  we might make. In that context I
therefore worry about what we might be doing in terms of greater cooperation. I would
hate to think we are in a position where the particular circumstances we are properly
concerned about with regard to the rise of ISIS ar e being used as a cover or an excuse
for a more broadening extension of intelligence powers and practices than might
otherwise have been the case. I have not heard that suggested, and I hope it is not, in
fact, the reality.
I think that for many people, what they have seen in recent weeks has really jolted
their attention in terms of the march of international terrorism, and it has given us a new
sense of how small and vulnerable our world is. The romantic notions that perhap s our
grandparents might have told us about, the troops that marched off to be part of the
international battalion during the Spanish Civil War and the fight against Franco and
fascism, do not apply today. Communication is more instant. Communication is mo re
sinister. Planning is more devious. It is not some romantic march for freedom, as those
fighters in the international battalion might have been on in the 1930s. So it is
appropriate for States to do things to protect themselves and their citizenry from the
threat of such attacks. The numbers for New Zealand may well be small, but those
people have contacts. Those people are a relatively fluid group, and we know they do
not simply sit around and talk just to each other; they talk to a range of other people.
I think that that is where we as citizens have a right to be both concerned and then
assured that the appropriate steps are being taken to protect our safety as individuals and
also our safety as a nation. We have seen examples in other countries of qu ite random
and quite significant —in the sense of particular —attacks on individuals. It is not so
much a case of the grand attack any more, it seems to me, but a much more immediate,
random attack that cuts at the very core of the confidence of a society. B e it plans for
moves in Australia that have been thwarted or be it the assassination of innocent
citizens in Canada or in the United Kingdom, the risk is none the less the same. So the
issue for New Zealand is what we can do to protect our citizens in that  respect. The
safeguard we have is that the measures that have been announced are, in my view,
prudent and will also be examined by a select committee before they are passed by this
House.
I want to say this to the Prime Minister. I think it was a good st ep to make the
statement in the way he did this morning. I think that if there are to be future iterations
of this process, they should be made in the same way to this Parliament, where they can
be debated and a consensus secured for the measures that we m ight be about to take,
because the best way of securing our freedom for the future is to ensure that we have all
bought into the concept of what it is we are trying to secure, right from the outset.
Frankly, a divided House or a divided country in these so rts of situations leaves us
nowhere. So I think that today is a useful start. There is a lot of ground yet to cover, and
I look forward to further discussions and debate as the tides continue to flow.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I rise on behalf of the ACT Party in support
of the proposals announced this morning. My party believes that the first and most
important role of the State is to protect citizens against thugs. This duty applies whether
the thugs reside overseas or within our borders. Given this extraordinary power,
however, the State does have a tendency to overreach. Over the past century, much of
classical liberals’ attention has been rightly focused on resisting the overreach of the
State. That was right, I say, because those Governments did suppress freedom of
movement and freedom of contract. Many of my remarks are directed at civil
libertarians, of whom I count myself as one, unlike some of the more ostentatious
appeals to that constituency made earlier.
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 621
Actually, I want to congratul ate the Prime Minister and the acting deputy l eader of
the Labour Party on very fine speeches. I began to appreciate some of the opponents of
MMP until I saw that Peter Dunne made a very fine speech too.
We support the intention to ensure that proper parliamentary processes are followed,
even while we  are, for very good reason, speeding them up a little. We support the
moves to tidy up inconsistencies between the powers of the police and the SIS,
inconsistencies that unduly hamper justified monitoring of internal threats. The other
moves—the funding boost to the SIS, the changes in respect of passports, the narrow
changes to emergency surveillance, and the sunset clauses —all appear to be measured
and restrained in scope.
But the issues being considered today go well beyond those internal matters, and
they do so because it is not always the State that is a threat to liberty, or even other
States that are the threat. The contest in the Middle East and the threa ts of global
terrorism in recent decades have come from stateless entities —or, at least, currently
stateless entities, as their ambition is to create their own State. We need hardly debate
whether there is a contest of values at stake in respect of the Isl amic State of Iraq and
the Levant (ISIL). That entity represents the antithesis of civilised values—the values of
liberty, the rule of law, freedom of association, freedom of religion, and democratic
institutions.
But the question is whether we should get  involved at all. As a country we have
throughout our history played our part in defending not just borders but also the values
of free and democratic societies and of modern civilisation. It is true that the military
contest in the Middle East is not our fight in so far as they are not our borders, but the
contest about the kind of society that will prevail in that region is of profound interest
and concern to free societies everywhere. Here the issue is very much a contest of
values, the spread of those v alues around the world, and the threat those values are to
free and open societies.
We do not need to document or list the brutalities of ISIL. We have seen them on the
news most nights. ISIL does pose a threat to the people of Iraq and Syria and the
broader Middle East. Its current operational threats are in the Middle East and North
Africa, but its declared threats are global, and specifically directed at Western liberal
democracies. They are not just theoretical threats. As we have seen in Australia and
Canada recently, ISIL’s adherents and supporters are capable of random acts of
violence. The scale may so far be small but their aspirations are not.
One option might be to sit back and wait to see what else ISIL is capable of. We
could wait until its ca pability either wanes or others more directly affected work to
ensure ISIL is defeated, or wait until it succeeds in a violent provocation of sufficient
scale that a military response becomes the only option. It is not at all clear whether for
free societies generally a purely defensive posture is possible, at least not if we wish to
maintain a free and open society in our world. A purely defensive posture would be a
garrison State, the wagons circled, a wall put up, with extensive and intrusive
surveillance within. That is not the free and open society so painfully built and fought
for through the past century and before. And that is, simply, the case for playing our
part and contributing.
We would all much rather that none of this was necessary. New Zeala nd is a small
country well away from the immediate theatre of struggle in the Middle East. In a direct
sense, this is not our fight. They are not our borders at threat. But the values at stake are
our values. Although the aspirations of ISIL do not reach o ur shores, they affect our
way of life. So the case for playing our part, however small that might be, is a strong
one. Is helping those directly at threat from ISIL a worthy goal, the morally right thing
to do? Yes, it is unambiguously so. Is stopping ISI L achievable? With a broad
622 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
international contribution, the answer must surely be yes, because it has to be. To allow
a stateless gang, one utterly pitted against our freedoms and way of life, to dominate a
large swath of territory in the Middle East as a l aunching pad for broader aspirations is
unthinkable. In that sense, the situation in Iraq and Syria has direct relevance for our
domestic security, our values, and our economy as a small trading nation dependent on
international trade and the rule of law internationally.
For New Zealand to make a small contribution to international efforts to prevent the
humanitarian crisis from deepening and to support the capabilities of those directly in
the firing line seems a justifiable and proportionate response ent irely in keeping with
our traditional values. We must, of course, be aware of unintended consequences —of
mission creep, as they say. From what the Prime Minister has said, no more is being
contemplated than humanitarian aid and capacity building for crucia l Iraqi institutions,
including the army. The ACT Party can support these limited and proportionate
measures. They signal a willingness by New Zealand to play our part. The question that
matters is whether this is a struggle that is warranted. From what we  know so far, it is,
thus we support the limited moves announced today and the intention to seek broad
political support for them and to pursue due process in implementing them. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: This debate this afternoon is
somewhat unusual in so much as it is usually the case, in a ministerial statement, that
only the leaders of parties of more than six members are able to make a contribution.
The Business Committee made a decision yesterday that it should be a broad debate
because of its nature. That was a decision made unanimously by all members of the
Business Committee. I do want to make that statement so that those who might be
observing t he debate realise that all of Parliament recognises the gravity of the
announcement made by the Prime Minister today.
We are having this debate because the Government is responding to a threat from the
Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. I think what is  missing a little bit in some of the
commentary this afternoon is that this is an organisation that respects no boundaries.
This is an organisation that has declared a caliphate and that has a big reach into
countries throughout the world, calling on disaf fected people who would want to
somehow support it to engage in terrorist activities. The numbers that were given by the
Prime Minister in his speech today—somewhat unusually, I might add—indicate that its
reach has reached our shores as well as the shores  of many other countries. So for us to
turn a blind eye and say that we are a country that respects freedom and we are a peace -
loving country that respects people’s abilities to do whatever they like would be to put
at risk the lives of New Zealanders, wit hout recognising that those whom we seek to
protect—in the case of the contributions made by one party here today —would be the
very people who would seek to destroy the freedoms that we have.
I just have to make a comment about the headline that is curren tly running on the
Fairfax website. It says that we are at war. I think that is an extremely irresponsible
headline to have run. I think that the four journalists who have attached their names to it
need to reconsider the offering that they are putting in front of the public, in light of the
full speech that they listened to, given by the Prime Minister. This is not a war in a
conventional sense at all. This is about New Zealand taking some steps to protect New
Zealanders here in our own country. When it co mes to the objections that people might
want to raise about military personnel looking at what we might do in regard to
capacity-building in Iraq, let us be clear that legitimate Governments in all countries
around the world contribute to our general secur ity. New Zealanders travel a lot. New
Zealanders are in many countries throughout the world, and in all of those places, if this
organisation is allowed to run rampant, then their security is compromised.
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 623
There have been suggestions today that some of the  information that has come out
has been in the form of a hint. I think Annette King said it was a drip -feed with a small
amount of humanitarian aid, and the Rt Hon Winston Peters suggested that it was
lacking detail, yet at the same time called for caution . That was also the theme from
Annette King. In a way they are both right, because this has been an evolving situation.
If you went back 12 months, this is an organisation that no one had really heard of. Yet
in that short period of time, the reign of terror that it has inflicted upon the world is such
that has never been seen before.
I wonder how anyone can promote the idea that there can be an organisation in the
world that respects no boundaries, that encourages domestic terrorism at large, that
videos and promulgates its activities—killing and beheading innocent people, etc. —and
that can somehow not be considered a threat to us here in New Zealand.
I do though want to thank the Labour Party, the New Zealand First Party, the Māori
Party, the ACT Party, and United Future for saying that they will support those extra
moves for us to deal with the intelligence community throughout the world. My
colleague will speak further on that. We will also engage in diplomacy, whenever
possible, to try to make a difference. But in the end it is going to be the countries that
are most affected by this, and, initially, Iraq, that need to stand up and do the business of
putting this group of people—I hesitate to use the terms “ISIL” or even “Islamic State”,
because it implies that all those who are followers of Islam are somehow marked by
this. That is not something I believe or that anyone in this Parliament, I am sure,  would
believe.
This terrorist organisation does need to be stopped, and a first port of call, it would
seem, would be for Iraq itself to be able to have the strength to overcome the oppression
of these people. We do have some people in the Middle East wh o are looking at what
we might be able to do to assist with that. I reject the statement by Winston Peters that a
decision has been made. It has not, but without good information, without on -the-
ground intelligence, and without a decent assessment of what is possible, we could not
make a decision. It would be, I think, remiss of us to simply rely on information that we
got from others. Yes, we have some people who are going to make some inquiries on
our behalf, and I think that that is totally appropriate.
I just make the point that we do have to be a great deal more vigilant, given what we
now all know from the Prime Minister’s speech this morning. We will have to make
some law changes, but we do have to be incredibly careful that the caution we now start
to take in expanding that vigilance does not start to impinge upon the freedoms of law -
abiding New Zealanders. I think, conversely, law-abiding New Zealanders would expect
us to keep their lives free and safe from this sort of threat.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I join with others in thanking the
Government for opening up this opportunity to discuss this very important issue. We do
face an uncertain world, and the brutality and the atrocities of the Islamic State of Iraq
and Syria (ISIS) is part of that, but obvi ously not the only issue. There are threats to
New Zealand and we have to acknowledge that. We have said, as Annette King said
before, that we will adopt a bipartisan approach to strengthening, where necessary, New
Zealand SIS. We appreciate, again, the op portunity to be briefed on that. But we will
also reserve our final comment until we actually see that legislation before us. Where
there are gaps, obviously we will need to plug them, but we also need to be vigilant
because this is ultimately about the ba lancing of our security with our human rights.
Select committee consideration, as we have insisted upon, is a critical issue. The option
of urgency is not acceptable. I was also pleased to see the sunset clause, which means
that this legislation will ultimately fade out as the review of the legislation goes ahead.
624 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
I want to make the point that we have to be very, very careful here that we do not
overstate the issue of the threat that is before us. We have just heard Gerry Brownlee
talk about this as being the worst terrorist organisation in history. John Key said last
week that ISIS will “rain carnage on the world”. Make no mistake, it is a nasty, brutish
organisation that violates human rights in an awful way. But is ISIS about to bring
mayhem and terror i nto our neighbourhoods? The answer is no. It is brutal. It does
commit atrocities and it uses those as a weapon to dominate two countries —Syria and
Iraq—and it is sophisticated in the way that it uses local people to take up arms.
We need to be very carefu l—very careful—about what we do to our local Muslim
population, which is a productive and peace -loving part of our community. We are in
some ways radicalising those people —in ways that we do not know how they could be
radicalised—by the actions we take. I am mindful of a study by the Royal United
Services Institute in the UK, which was looking at the UK’s role in the Iraq war. It said
that that role increased the radicalisation of young Muslims. It said that far from
reducing international terrorism, the 20 03 invasion had the effect of promoting it. If the
cause is right, then we accept whatever risk we take, but we should understand that
whatever we get into will affect the security of us back here in New Zealand.
The Prime Minister also argues that this i s an international, a regional, and a local
problem. I do not agree. This is a conflict that should be contained locally and
regionally, but it is actually we who are internationalising it by our presence in that
local and regional area. If we contrast the  Islamic State with al -Qaeda, for example, al -
Qaeda actually started the other way. It internationalised a Muslim or an Islamic issue,
rather than doing it locally. Arguably, in 2001 it posed a much greater risk than the
Islamic State does today. The Islam ic State is not threatening the world. Again, I am
mindful, looking back in history to 2002, of when Tony Blair and his Cabinet said that
Iraq posed an imminent threat to Britain. That is fairly laughable today, but it was the
rhetoric at the time that was  used to justify the Iraq war. We should take real care that
we do not exaggerate the threat of ISIS to justify the action that we are taking in New
Zealand.
Let us look at the broader contribution to Iraq. On the issue of Iraq, this Government
appears to be driven by the desire to do something alongside our “Five Eyes” partners.
The rhetoric was somewhat dialled back immediately after the election, when John Key
was talking about deploying the SAS. So New Zealand’s possible military contribution,
as announced, is a sort of balance between doing something to be there and, on the other
hand, not upsetting the New Zealand public. The Prime Minister has probably looked at
some of the polling data that has been coming through. If he has, he would realise that
New Zealanders actually see sending our young people off to war when there is little
understanding of what they are there to do or what they are there to achieve as folly.
They might be right to ask those questions and have those doubts about what the
reasons would be. If you look at what military analysts are saying about the current
tactic of airstrikes, they are saying that those will not work without boots on the ground.
We should remember, actually, that the forerunner of ISIS was what we called al -
Qaeda in Iraq. Al-Qaeda in Iraq was actually defeated by the surge, it was called, of tens
of thousands of American soldiers alongside the arming of local Iraqi tribesmen —the
same sort of tribesmen who fought valiantly but were defeated and then brutally
murdered just this week by ISIS when they were trying to stand up for their freedoms
but were not given the weaponry and the support that they needed. That points to the
problems within Iraq rather than the problems of outsiders trying to do the job.
If we are going to go into Iraq, then we need to make a contribution, and a sensible
one. We appear today to be emphasising a more military solution. There was talk about
sending nine people into Iraq. We already know that three have gone, so we have made
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 625
this dec ision despite the fact that we have made no decisions! We have made this
decision already in terms of who we are sending off to Baghdad. I can be pretty
emphatic that those people coming back will not be saying there is nothing for us to do
there. They will be coming back with a job for the military. We have to balance that off
with the risk that we face by becoming involved in even the most benign form of
contribution militarily—that we then slide further into additional deployments, that we
up the risk of  our own insecurity. Most of all, we have to be looking at what we will
achieve. I do not believe that the contribution of some military trainers, frankly, will
achieve very much. Let us remember that the US spent 10 years in Iraq and spent
billions of dol lars training an entire Iraqi army only to have it collapse in the first
assault that it faced. This is not something, I believe, that we are going to contribute
meaningfully in and around. The army itself was not the problem; it was the way Prime
Minister al-Maliki at the time favoured his Shi’a group, and, in a sense, undermined the
very confidence that the Sunn is had in the work of the Shia . That was commented on
today by the Prime Minister in passing.
In terms of the diplomatic role that we can play, I  believe we can play a much more
positive role in strengthening the Government, the judiciary, and the political
framework that is operating in Iraq. We should seek a United Nations Security Council
resolution for a mandate to have forces on the ground, an d we should be able to up our
humanitarian contribution from the $1 million announcement today. We should be
focusing on those areas of ISIS where there is vulnerability. It is paying thousands and
thousands of military and administrators at the moment. It  needs money. It needs oil
revenues. We should be shutting off those possibilities of that revenue —oil coming out
and armed shipments going in. We should be looking at the difference we can make to
Iraq.
New Zealand has never hesitated to go into conflict s where we believed the cause
was right or where we were standing up for human rights or humanitarian law —
Afghanistan and Timor -Leste being the two most recent. But we have to question the
contribution that we make and whether it might be effective. There are consequences
that might flow from our actions that we cannot see or perceive today. We need to be
operating under a clear mandate. Our position on the United Nations Security Council
and the confidence that the world has shown in us in voting us on giv e us ample
opportunity to be able to do that.

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: About 2 weeks ago
from today I received a message at about 5 o’clock in t he morning to tell me about the
attack by a gunman in the House of Parliament in Canada. A short time later, I rang our
High Commissioner Simon Tucker, who was in the New Zealand High Commission
about two blocks from the Canadian Parliament, which was part  of the lockdown that
was in place at that time. When I asked him about the scene there, he said to me: “Well,
just imagine this was happening in the New Zealand Parliament, because the layout is
about the same.” He said it was like someone had taken out a  guard at the Supreme
Court—just down that way—hijacked a car to the front steps of Parliament, and, with a
gun, burst in the front door. He said that was pretty much the scene that was taking
place in Canada that day. The air of disbelief that was present in Canada on that day was
about the same as the air of disbelief you would expect if it had happened in this
country.
Members do not need me to tell them that the threat that we are here to discuss today
is a new and very dangerous one for countries like ours. Nor should I need to remind
members that the individual responsible for that act in Canada was a person who had
been newly radicalised and who had been denied the opportunity to commit jihad in the
626 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
Middle East and had instead turned his mind to steps  of violence that could be
undertaken where he was.
The advent of a well -resourced, globally focused, internet -savvy terrorist group,
skilled at preying on the vulnerabilities of the disturbed and disenfranchised, is a new
and very dangerous phenomenon fo r countries like ours. As we have heard today, we
now live in a country where there are individuals who have access to these websites —
no doubt many of them are disturbed and disenfranchised —who have become
radicalised, and have planned to go to the Middle East and commit acts of violence
there. Some have gone, as the Prime Minister has told us today, to Syria. We know that
there are others who have been denied the opportunity to go to the Middle East and who
remain here. No doubt some of them, like that per son in Canada, are reflecting on acts
of violence that can be undertaken here instead of those they had intended to undertake
in the Middle East.
I want to support the words of the Hon Annette King in relation to the UN Security
Council resolution on foreign fighters. In fact, I attended the beginning of that debate in
New York, and I believe that we should listen carefully to what was said there and heed
the instructions from the Security Council. It is important that New Zealand plays its
part by identifying the individuals who might export violence from here to places where
there is already rather too much of it, preventing them from going, and then turning our
minds to how we can make New Zealanders safe in a situation where those people will
then turn their minds to acts of violence in this country. The reminder we have seen in
Canada is one that we should heed in this country. I accept what Mr David Shearer said
to the Parliament. We should not over -egg the situation. We do not need to try to read
more into it than exists. But we do need to understand that there is a challenge here for
our society to deal with. We need to be careful that we confront it in a way that does not
make it worse, by making those who are targeted, who are identified, feel more
marginalised and therefore more a prospect of being radicalised.
I want to commend the balanced way in which most parties have received the
address from the Prime Minister today and the way in which other parties have
undertaken to consider constructively the recommendations that have been made. There
are always challenges when trying to find the right balance between the responsibility to
respect human rights and civil liberties on the one hand, and the need to protect the
public on the other. Finding tha t balance can only benefit from the scrutiny of members
of Parliament in the select committee and on the floor of the House.
I want to pick up the sentiment that has been raised by some members about the need
for New Zealand to do more on the humanitarian  front. As the Prime Minister has told
us today, we have committed about $13.5 million —add to that another $1 million
today—to a range of initiatives to try to alleviate the suffering of those who have been
displaced and disadvantaged in the Middle East. W e have worked, and will continue to
work, with a range of organisations, such as the United Nations High Commissioner for
Refugees, Unicef, the Red Cross, the World Food Programme, and UN relief works
agencies, as well as a range of NGOs. Anyone who has be en to any of the refugee
camps, as I have, will know the scale of the challenge that confronts the people there.
We need to do our part, on an ongoing basis.
In Turkey we have taken a rather different approach. We have engaged in bilateral
programmes with the Government of Turkey to construct schools in the refugee camps
of that country. Increasingly, we need to look for bilateral options to work with
countries facing this challenge. The region I mention particularly is Jordan, the smallest
of those countries, with I think a million and a half refugees now to contend with. This
is a country that is at risk of being truly swamped by the challenge that now confronts it.
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 627
I heard the words of the co -leader of the Green Party suggesting that there was no
role for military action in relation to Iraq. I simply say to her that those words will give
no comfort to the people in towns like Kobani or any of the other towns across Iraq
where we have seen cold -blooded killers and people engaged in torture, engaged in the
destruction of a very large piece of territory across Iraq and Syria. Once there is a space
created through military action —and I believe that the actions that have been
undertaken by other countries in that respect do need to be seen in a positive light, given
the risk confronting some of the communities there —there will be a need to look at
areas for capacity -building and support in Iraq, in particular. We need to remind
ourselves that the seeds of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant were sown when we
saw the Maliki Government in Iraq turn on too many of its own people, showing a lack
of respect for their human rights, and engaging in acts—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Sown in 2003.

items.speaker: Hon MURRAY McCULLY
items.text: Well, there is a long history there, as Mr Goff reminds
us, and I say simply that we need to be ready to do some work in the capacity -building
area. I agree with what Mr Shearer said about the need to look at law and justice
agencies, and areas of that sort, once we do see the oppor tunity to move beyond the
current conflict.
I just want, finally, to recognise the words of those who have referred to New
Zealand’s role on the UN Security Council from 1 January 2015. It is not until 1
January that we take up the new seat on the UN Secu rity Council, but, like others, I was
delighted to see three -quarters of the countries in the world support New Zealand for a
seat on the council. But with that support goes a very great sense of responsibility.
If you look at the key conflicts in the Mid dle East, the UN Security Council has been
a bystander for far too many years. If you look at what happened in Syria in recent
times, the UN Security Council was a bystander by reason of the veto used by more
than one of the permanent members of the counci l. As we have seen in relation to the
Iran nuclear file, the UN Security Council has very largely been a bystander on that
issue as we have seen the P5+1 process take place outside the UN environment. And, of
course, in relation to the Middle East peace pr ocess as a whole, we have seen a very
good resolution passed, I think, some 47 years ago, but no real action to breathe life into
that resolution to create a longstanding basis for peace in the Middle East.
So I say to members of the House taking the longer-term view that New Zealand as a
new member of the UN Security Council must commit itself to working with other
countries to create a Security Council environment where these challenges are no longer
ignored and where the big countries in the world confront their responsibilities.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: I have listened closely to the Prime Minister’s
statement this morning and to this debate on  New Zealand’s engagement towards the
Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL). In my contribution I want to focus on the
broader aspect of the ISIL situation —namely, the international action there and New
Zealand’s policy on that. We note the Government’s decision not to send SAS troops to
Iraq and we support that, but in answering questions after his speech, the Prime Minister
said his Government supported the coalition’s military action against ISIL —and that is
the elephant in the Chamber. So this House must address the question of the legal
validity and the political merit—or not—of military action against ISIL. Should there be
an international armed force against ISIL and should New Zealand support it? Our
answer, with respect, is no. Let me convey our reasoning.
We have asked ourselves five qu estions and they are these. Does ISIL comprise a
threat to peace and security that warrants responsive action of some kind by the
international community? If so, should that response include military action? If so, is
New Zealand obliged to join that milit ary action? If not, should it decide to do so on a
628 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
discretionary basis? If not, what other action might New Zealand take that is substantive
and constructive?
The Greens agree that ISIL poses a threat to peace and security. This is established in
Security Council Resolution 2170 of 15 August, adopted under article 39. It is based on
a judgment that ISIL is a terrorist organisation, which, on 2 July, declared itself to be
the Islamic State with universal jurisdiction over all Muslims everywhere. It has said
that: “The legality of all emirates, groups, states and organisations becomes null by the
expansion of the caliph’s authority …”. ISIL has also launched genocidal campaigns
against the Yezidi and Kurdish peoples. Its preferred method of political contesta tion is
the beheading of journalists in the desert. These actions warrant prosecution by the
International Criminal Court and a response under the responsibility to protect doctrine.
So an appropriate response by the international community is required.
Should that response include military action? Resolution 2170 called upon UN
member States to take all measures necessary and appropriate against ISIL, in
accordance with international law. The resolution was adopted unanimously under
chapter 7, but Russia stated that the resolution did not constitute authority for military
action. In situations of crisis, Security Council resolutions contain what is
diplomatically termed “constructive ambiguity”, which enables those preferring military
action to claim authorisation, and those opposing it to deny such authorisation.
Of course, military action has in fact been undertaken by eight Western and four
