Arab States. The United States, leading the military coalition, is claiming Iraq’s formal
request for collective self -defence under article 51, which is an inherent right that  does
not require council authorisation anyway. That self-defence claim, however, covers Iraq
but not Syria, which has not made such a request. So, with Syria, is the coalition
claiming resolution 2170 or the responsibility to protect doctrine as a justifi cation? The
coalition owes a formal explanation to the world as to the legal basis of their actions.
Is New Zealand obliged to join any military action, even if it were legally valid? The
short answer is no. Under the charter, we have an obligation to res pect binding
decisions of the council and not work against them, but without any formal agreements
concluded under article 43, we are not obliged to participate in any military actions,
even those authorised by the council. That requires a separate and sov ereign decision on
our own part. Should New Zealand, then, participate in such military action? That is a
political judgment and our answer is no.
The use of force by New Zealand can be justified in three ways. The first is narrow
nationalism—to defend our country, our own territory, and nothing else. The second is
broad nationalism —to defend our national security by deploying troops overseas to
avert a domestic threat back home. The third is internationalism —to participate in
collective force and to maintain peace and security, even if the threat to ourselves down
here is distant. In supporting the coalition action the Prime Minister is advancing a
justification based on the second and third of these. He is effectively saying that Islamic
radicalisation, including some Kiwis returned from jihad, poses an unacceptable threat
of violence here, and that to avert that we must assist in stopping and eradicating the
Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) over there. But this broad nationalism is mixed
with a call to support allies. There is not a word about UN authorisation.
The Greens’ view is different again. We apply the political criteria for the use of
force under the responsibility to protect doctrine endorsed by the United Nations
General Assembly. These q uestions have to be answered. Is the causal threshold for
action against ISIL met? If so, is the intention of the coalition States right? If so, are we
at the stage where the last resort of military action has genuinely arrived? If so, are air
strikes proportional to the threat posed by ISIL? If so, is there a reasonable prospect of
success in halting the suffering inflicted by ISIL or are the consequences of military
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 629
action there likely to be worse than inaction? A genuine application of these criteria
makes it clear to us that the use of force against ISIL is not justifiable. Reasonable
people may differ over these questions. I acknowledge that those arguing against
military action must advance credible alternative strategies to eliminate the threat of
ISIL, but that applies to all forms of terrorism. We look to the 2006 UN global counter -
terrorism strategy, which says to look first at the causes of the problem and work on
them.
So, equally, where is the reasoning process by which the coalition States have come
to the conclusions they have? Where is the debate in the Security Council that explores
these issues transparently? I have scrutinised the council debate behind Resolutions
2170 and 2178, which were adopted within the last 3 months. The debate does no t
reflect this degree of transparency. Where is the written opinion from our own Attorney-
General, tabled before this House, affirming the legality of such military action? Where
is the accompanying paper tabled by the Prime Minister setting out the politi cal case,
essentially meeting the above criteria I mentioned? There will be a Cabinet paper. Why
not release the Cabinet paper so that members of the legislature can explore and debate
the considerations entertained?
I am no stranger to crises. I worked a s a Kiwi diplomat on the Thailand -Cambodia
border in the early 1980s. I took parliamentarian missions into Haiti and Burundi during
the height of their domestic crises. I have visited Gaza and the West Bank and
witnessed house demolitions. I have travelled  in the Syrian eastern desert as the clouds
of war of 2003 were forming. I have experienced riots in Jordan during the days of 9/11.
I have recently visited the refugee camps on the Jordan border with Syria. I know how
emotion and rationality wage war in the human psyche when we are under severe strain,
both individually and collectively. Nothing in my personal experience persuades me
that military action is the politically wise response. It requires diplomatic negotiation
towards a durable political settle ment, supported by humanitarian aid. We should not
support any military action against ISIS.

items.speaker: DARROCH BALL
items.text: As the New Zealand First leader, the Rt Hon
Winston Peters, has outlined, we welco me the statement from the Prime Minister today
on New Zealand’s response to the serious threat from Islamic State (IS). We do believe
that the Prime Minister has been less than forthright. Now —finally—we have a
statement in which we are told that 10 milita ry planners will be going to Iraq. As soon
as one of those military professionals arrives in Iraq, there can be no doubt that New
Zealand has committed to being involved in a new conflict. Some may already be there.
We understand that three left yesterday, though the PM claimed on the same day that no
decisions about Iraq had been made. With our foot in the door, there is no going back. It
is quite clear which side we are on. From the Islamic State point of view, that means we
are the enemy. To suggest that we are not part of this conflict because we are not putting
in combat forces is double-speak.
The Prime Minister is trying to disguise his intentions. What is the point about not
being clear? We are going to be represented in Iraq. We will be in an active campaign to
defeat IS. The Prime Minister does acknowledge that IS will be difficult to get rid of.
This might be a long campaign. The Government must, then, put New Zealanders at
ease about the state of our Defence Force. Is it up to scratch? Is it up t o the job we are
giving the armed forces to do? Because if there is a long conflict, we may become
further involved, if not in Iraq then somewhere else. Are our forces well -equipped? Can
they meet the challenges of deploying in another country with quite different terrain and
climate from ours? We have had too many reports about the failure of armed forces,
vehicles, and equipment. We want assurances that our Defence Force is in a state where
the men and women who will serve for us will not be let down by failing equipment.
630 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
As a former member of the New Zealand Army, I know about the great effort that
our servicemen and servicewomen put into all of their duties. Today we are discussing
matters of high national importance and security. There is a perspective that must not be
overlooked—that is, the situation of the men and women in the armed forces, whom we
rely on to represent New Zealand in whatever capacity we call on them. It is all very
well to talk about grand principles and broad diplomatic ideals, but , ultimately,
countering terrorism is about capability—personnel and resources. Our armed forces are
small, but they must be professional and well -equipped. That is an essential condition
that must underpin New Zealand’s response to global terrorism.
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister in charge of the NZ Security
Intelligence Service): I am taking a call in this House as Minis ter responsible for the
GCSB and Minister in charge of the NZ Security Intelligence Service. The Prime
Minister today gave a very important speech. He has said more than has ever been said
in this country about some of the security threats facing this nati on. Although there are
very good reasons that we cannot talk about everything our security agencies do, the
Prime Minister has made the remarks he has made today because within the limits on
what we can say, we intend to say and explain whatever we can, wh enever we can. The
threat to New Zealand from foreign fighters and would -be foreign fighters, to which the
Prime Minister has referred today, should not be a cause for alarm. It should, however,
serve as a reminder that the view that New Zealand exists in a benign strategic
environment is misguided. As Mr McCully has said, let us not think we are immune to
the threats posed to other Western countries. We have all seen the increase in
parliamentary security around these precincts over the past 2 weeks, and a  number of
people in this place will have visited the Canadian Parliament. The shock felt in Ottawa
2 weeks ago attests to the completely unexpected nature of the violence. The threats we
and our friends face are new threats, and we have to respond in a co nsidered manner,
but we must respond.
First, I want to endorse what other honourable members have said about
humanitarian assistance. I think Mrs King put it very well when she explained the
meeting that she and I had with members of the Iraqi community i n Wellington just a
couple of weeks ago. Their relatives are suffering greatly in places like Mosul and on
the Nineveh Plain, and desperately need our help and the help of other nations. In
deciding to look at this area, the Government has been very mindfu l not only of the
realities that face New Zealand but of our international obligations. Mrs King —rightly,
in my opinion—referred specifically to UN Security Council Resolution 2178, adopted
unanimously on 24 September 2014 under Chapter 7 of the United Nat ions Charter.
Among other things, the Security Council called on all member States, in accordance
with their obligations under international law, to cooperate in efforts to address the
threat posed by foreign terrorist fighters, including preventing foreig n terrorist fighters
from crossing their borders. The Security Council also emphasised the importance of
States ensuring that their domestic laws and regulations are fit for purpose in relation to
their nationals who travel or attempt to travel to a State “other than their States of
residence or nationality for the purpose of the perpetration, planning, or preparation of,
or participation in, terrorist acts or the providing or receiving of terrorist training,”.
The Greens have singularly failed to acknowle dge the substance of this resolution
this afternoon—hardly surprising but very disappointing. I am disappointed in Kennedy
Graham, who pretty well knows off by heart every United Nations Security Council
resolution when it suits him. But he did not address  key issues raised by this resolution.
New Zealand has legislation that, on paper at least, addresses these issues, but the
legislation is not perfect. It has gaps. It does not contain all the tools that we require.
Our actions to date are in accordance wi th our international obligations, but the
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 631
problems we confront are not ours alone. They span countries and they span borders.
We would be neglecting our responsibilities not to address them.
The Prime Minister has this morning announced a very measured se t of legislative
changes that will enable the security services more effectively to carry out their work.
He has also announced a $7 million financial boost for the SIS, which will ensure that it
can carry out the work we need it to do. For all the hyperbo le we have heard from the
usual suspects this afternoon, the changes announced are very measured. No new
criminal offences are being introduced. Several changes are being made to the law
relating to passport cancellation. Several changes will make it easie r for the New
Zealand SIS to carry out operational activities that most New Zealanders would
probably already think it is able to carry out.
I want to mention the proposal to give the SIS an emergency surveillance power to
conduct for no longer than 48 ho urs urgent surveillance before a warrant can be issued.
Some people will contend this change is a sweeping one, but it is not. They are wrong.
It is important to put the proposal in context. The proposal echoes the power already
given to certain authoritie s under section 48 of the Search and Surveillance Act 2012,
which provides that a “ device warrant need not be obtained for use of surveillance
device in some situations of emergency or urgency”. That Act has been in force for over
2 years and the sky has n ot fallen in. It is not envisaged that this power will be used
often by the SIS, but it is important that the SIS has the ability to investigate an
emergency situation where the circumstances require it. In order to use the power, the
SIS director will hav e to be satisfied that the threshold for issuing a warrant would be
met. The Prime Minister has also made clear this morning his expectation that the SIS
will report publicly on an annual basis outlining how many times it has used the power.

items.speaker: So take this hypothetical
items.text: an emergency situation arises. I am the Minister
responsible for the SIS. I am unavailable because I am in another part of the country. I
am not back in Wellington for, say, 20 hours. If the matter is not addressed within 20
hours the consequences are very serious. The urgent surveillance is undertaken and then
I return to Wellington to consider, along with the Commissioner of Security Warrants, a
warrant. If we do not agree that the surveillance was urgent or warranted, a warrant will
not be signed. The material must then be destroyed. There is a disincentive to use the
power for anything other than truly urgent situations.
I look forward to the important debate the House will have when the legislation is
introduced, and in debating the legis lation it should also be borne in mind that
Parliament will need to consider all our security legislation over the coming months. As
part of the extensive oversight measures introduced last year —and I acknowledge Mr
Dunne for his work on that matter —section 21 of the Intelligence and Security
Committee Act requires a “ review of the intelligence and security agencies, the
legislation governing them, and their oversight legislation  … [to] be commenced before
30 June 2015;”. That means a comprehensive review o f all relevant legislation. So there
will be a lot of work for this House to do in this area in the next 12 to 18 months. As I
said last week, there has to be robust debate. No proposition should go unchallenged.
Dissent can be a very good thing. It is in the public interest that members from all sides
work together to ensure the law, both substantive and procedural, is fit for purpose and
serves the interests of this country. That is why I hope the House will engage with the
detail of these proposals with an eye on ensuring a quality legislative product rather
than scoring political points.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: In some ways this is the sort of debate
that is the most important debate that we ever have in the House of Representatives, and
that is because we deal with fundamental responsibilities that we in this place have:
first, to safeguard our citizens against real or potential risks, and, second, to make a
632 Ministerial Statements 05 Nov 2014
decision about how a  nation like New Zealand should respond to the risks and the
threats created by the wider situation in the Middle East. I say the wider situation in the
Middle East because you cannot differentiate the threat that the Islamic State of Iraq and
Syria (ISIS) poses from the factors that have led to its creation, which are the appalling
humanitarian conditions that emanated from the oppression by Bashar al -Assad in Syria
on the one hand and the appalling things that were happening in Iraq, not only Sunni
against Shi’a but also Shi’a against Sunni.
So when we start to talk about the threats and the appalling brutality in the Middle
East, let us not pretend for a moment that we are talking about only one organisation,
ISIS. Yes, it is brutal. Yes, it is disgusting . Yes, it poses a potential threat. But I have to
say that it has killed nothing like the 200,000 people in Syria who have died because of
the actions of Bashar al -Assad. Equally, if you look at the problem in Iraq, it is not, as
the Minister of Foreign Af fairs stated before, simply something that resulted from the
al-Maliki prime ministership. It is something that goes back to the misguided decision
in 2003 to invade Iraq without proper preparation and without any examination of the
unintended consequences of that action.
I want to come back and divide my comments up into two parts. One is the question
of what threat might exist in New Zealand and how we respond to it, and the second is
how we should respond to that broader situation in the Middle East. Th e first thing I
have to say is that I welcome the fact that the Government has been more forthcoming
in terms of its proposals and sharing them with other political parties, but I do express
my regret that this legislation will be passed in the 2 weeks aft er we come back to the
House. That, in my view, is insufficient time for this House to give proper scrutiny to
the fundamental issues that are involved whenever you extend the powers of a security
intelligence organisation. I think that offsetting that is the fact that there will be a sunset
clause, so the Government has limited what it intends to put into that legislation, and
that at the insistence of the Labour Party there will be a truncated select committee
process, at least, so we can allow public and specialist input into the legislation.
I want to say that it is important that we are vigilant about the threats posed by
terrorism but that we should also be proportionate and balanced. I lived in the United
Kingdom at the time of the IRA terrorist atta cks. That threat was far more extensive
than anything that we have seen from ISIS. That is just a fact. I was working in the
Parliament buildings, in the House of Commons, and there was a real and present threat
to the lives of people living in the United Kingdom because of the actions of the IRA.
We did not, however, brand it with an ideology, such as calling it Islamic, and the
British Government dealt with it.
I have to say to the Prime Minister as well that I read his speech carefully and there
were things that I agreed with in the speech and things that I disagreed with. One was
the impression given that the international environment has become much less benign
over time. I was Minister of Foreign Affairs at the time of 9/11. I can tell you that when
we had a synchronised and coordinated attack that killed thousands of people in the
United States, it was bigger than anything I have felt from ISIS in New Zealand and
internationally. When the biggest country in the world closes its borders, it is not
benign. So let us see this in context. Yes, we should take ISIS seriously, but no, we
should not blow it out of proportion into something that it is not. I am also old enough
to remember the dark days of the Cold War when we had multiple nuclear weapons on
high alert and civilisation as we know it could have come to an end at any particular
occasion. So, yes, let us take the threats seriously, but let us keep it proportionate.
It is also important domestically not to go too far in the legislation, because we know
that what causes radicalising of a minority part of the population is when you create
conditions where they feel alienated and where they feel that they are being
05 Nov 2014 Ministerial Statements 633
discriminated against. I have got a significant Muslim population in my electorate of Mt
Roskill. I have known them for years. I have worked with them for years. I can say that
this is a group in my community that is hard working, peaceful, and law abiding. But if
we start to create the impression that Islamic equals terrorism and we start to  see New
Zealanders being abusive of Muslim people in this country, then we will create the very
conditions that we are setting out to avoid.
I have to say, from talking to many of my Muslim friends, that they are subject in the
street to increasing abuse  because of their appearance or their dress. So more important
than this legislation might be dealing with that situation. I acknowledge that John Key
said in his speech that our Muslim community is overwhelmingly positive and law
abiding. More important m ight be how we ensure that that community does not feel so
alienated from the community that it is part of that we create the conditions for action
by people with personality disorders.
I think that the moves that are made in the proposed legislation are not extreme
moves. We have the Search and Surveillance Act, and I cannot see why powers that are
available to the police might not be available to the SIS when confronting similar
situations, but, naturally, we want to be clear about the safeguards to prev ent the abuse
of that power. The reason we do not have visual surveillance provisions in the New
Zealand Security Intelligence Service Act is that I think it dates back to 1969.
I acknowledge that there might be some occasions when Attorney -General is not
available to sign a warrant, but we do live in the 21 st century, and I do not think it ever
takes 48 hours to get in touch with the Attorney -General. If it does, we would have to
wonder what he was up to and why. I think that in the select committee we ne ed to say
yes, there may be a provision where in an emergency situation the action takes place,
but no, we are not going to leave it for 48 hours before we regularise that warrant. That
is something that I hope we can look at in good faith in the select co mmittee
consideration.
I want to come, finally, to the question of passports. The right to travel freely is a
precious right, but it is not an absolute right. If we know somebody in New Zealand  is
about to head off and join an organisation that the UN reg ards as committing crimes
against humanity and war crimes —and it does not matter whether it is for ISIS or for
any other UN-designated terrorist organisation—then of course we have a responsibility
to stop that person. We should not, however, render people  stateless who are currently
travelling on passports. It is critical that if a person overseas loses their passport —if it is
taken away from them —then we have an immediate availability of travel documents to
allow them to return to New Zealand. I hope that is what the Government is proposing.
What I want to say finally about the contribution of the campaign against ISIS is that
there is a lot we can do on a humanitarian basis. We can make a difference. There are
millions of refugees. That is where we should be focusing. We can make a difference  in
our role on the United Nations Security Council. When we sit down in Washington with
other countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Turkey, who are part of the coalition of the
willing, and find out that the resources that ISIS is receiving —the money, t he people,
and the weapons—are coming from those very countries, then that is the place to start to
isolate ISIS and to defeat it. I am not at all convinced that military action is appropriate
in these circumstances. The road to hell is paved with good int entions. Yes, there might
have been good intentions to remove Saddam or to remove Gaddafi, but as a result of
misguided efforts by the West hundreds of thousands of innocent people lost their lives
and we ended up with a situation much worse than it was ev en under those oppressive
regimes. We should be very wary of entering in a military capacity in any sense into
that conflict in the Middle East.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Allow me to take just a couple of moments,
firstly to thank the House for what I think was a very constructive debate. I think the
situation that we face and the threats that we face from the  Islamic State of Iraq and
Syria (ISIS) warrant the careful consideration that the House has given it this afternoon
and the mature and intelligent debate that people have added.
Let me give parties an absolute assurance that the select committee debate will
literally be that—an opportunity to test out the proposed changes that the Government is
making. As we have said, they will be narrowly focused and, as I think a number of
speakers have pointed out, they are appropriately set. We acknowledge that the 48 -hour
issue is something that needs to be carefully considered and carefully monitored.
The point, really, around the 48 hours —if I can make this point —is simply that it
does take a little longer to raise a warrant, not because the Attorney -General is not
available to sign it in his capacity as the Minister responsible; it is because the
commissioner takes a very long period of time, and rightfully so, to very thoughtfully
go through a warrant. So when the commissioner turns up, he —as has been the case
with Sir John Jeffries and now Sir Bruce Robertson —actually spends an approp riate
period of time making absolutely sure that that warrant should be raised. So the only
point here really is that sometimes that process —if by chance of the way of information
that came to us, we were to hear something that we felt we needed to act on very, very
quickly, that is the rare and exceptional circumstance. And really, unless the SIS were
absolutely convinced that warrant could be raised, it would be ridiculous for the SIS to
actually go on an exercise of gathering information, because they wo uld have to destroy
it. They would not be able to use it. Actually, I think it would damage their reputation if
we started having the SIS going out and saying that they had constantly been
undertaking this 48 -hour surveillance. But look, I think it is one of those things
Parliament should kick around, and we will take those discussions in good faith. So that
is really the main issue there.
In terms of the final point, I would simply make this point in relation to the
Government’s suggestion of what we shou ld be doing on the ground in Iraq. I share the
view with those who say that in the end the situation in Iraq has to be resolved with the
Iraqis. It actually has to be resolved with a Government that recognises not a secular
response to this but an inclusiv e response. Ultimately, unless the Sunnis, the Shi’as and
the Kurds are listened to and they feel as if they are included, a long -term solution in
Iraq will never be found. It will not matter how much military effort you put in, it will
not resolve it.
So the Iraqis have to fight their own battles, and actually they have to find a
diplomatic way through. But it will be necessary, ultimately, to combat the Islamic State
of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL), and that is clearly on display. We saw that yesterday
when ISIL essentially executed 322 people —women and children. We cannot let that
happen unanswered. The Government is trying to take a careful but measured response.
But I think putting our SAS in on the ground as some sort of killing machine would not
work as a long-term solution. I think in the end Iraq has to be the owner of its own long-
term problems. We are here to help, but I do not think we can fight its battles for it.

1. Hon ANNETTE KING (Acting Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Prime

items.speaker: Minister

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In the Speech from the Throne, he stated that his Government’s
plan includes higher incomes for New Zealanders. What percentage wage movement

items.text: One that is in excess of the inflation rate.

items.text: In light of that, does he think an increase of 70 percent a year

items.text: I assume the member is talking about some of the pay
increases that chief executives at mixed -ownership model companies have received. I
do not know the composition and make -up of the ir pay, but I suspect that in fact what
has really happened is they have not had a 70 percent increase in their salary; they have
probably had a combination of stock options and other parts of their payment, and also
an incentive payment reflecting the per formance of the company. Actually, you do get
those kinds of moves —both up and down —with chief executives, but that is not
something that goes in terms of just their straight salary increase.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How does the Government just ify a pay increase of 70 percent,
or $900,000, for the chief executive officer of Mighty River Power as just a market
correction, but a $2 an hour increase of the minimum wage paid to the lowest -paid New

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The Government does not justify it, because the justification is
required by the board of directors and the chairman of the company. Actually, I have
not done this exercise, but if members opposite want me to, I will go away and have a
look at the incentive payments made to other chief executives under the previous
Labour Government. I am pretty sure you will find that when Meridian Energy was run
by Keith Turner, 16 percent of the company was sold in the form of Southern Hydro,
and there were p roceeds of $1.5 billion and a $600,000 million profit. I may be wrong,

items.text: Does he stand by his statement: “We’d prefer that we were a

Child Poverty—School Food Programmes
2. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement to Radio New
Zealand on 22 October that about 15 percent of kids in decile 1 to 4 schools were
“clearly in need” of breakfast at school for a variety of reasons, including “they are
unsure if they are going to get a lot of lunch or dinner”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOH N KEY
items.text: Yes, but if the member was to quote me from the entire
interview, she will also acknowledge that what I said was that was a very anecdotal
number.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What do principals tell him are the reasons why children come to
school without breakfast or lunch?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Truthfully, there is a wide variety of reasons, but it is not for
me to analyse them. What it is for me to do is to show leadership, and that is exactly
what the Government did in partnering w ith Fonterra and Sanitarium to provide
breakfast in schools for every child who wanted it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister believe that the State should also provide
lunch at school for the 15 percent of children in decile 1 to 4 sch ools, whom he has said
are clearly in need, if their parents cannot, for whatever reason, provide them with that
lunch?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not believe that the number of children who go to decile 1
to 4 schools who do not have lunch is  15 percent. I have asked extensively at the decile
1, 2, 3, and 4 schools I have been to. Quite a number of principals actually even reject
the notion that they need breakfast in schools. Those who do take breakfasts in schools
tell me that for the odd child who does not have lunch, they either give them some more
breakfast or provide them with lunch. But what they have said to me is that the number
of children in those schools who actually require lunch is the odd one or two.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Prime Minister believe that the State has a responsibility to
provide food—breakfast and lunch —for hungry children in schools, when their parents
cannot, for whatever reason, provide it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I believe that parents have a responsibility to provide lunch.
What I do acknowledge is that sometimes schools will provide a lunch if one is not
provided. As I said to the member just before, the evidence I see from the principals I
ask—I go to a lot of schools and I ask every principal that question, and I ask every
teacher I can that question—is that the number of children who turn up without lunch is
extremely few.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: If the parents cannot provide lunch and schools are unable to provide
lunch, and he will not have his Government provide lunch, then who will feed these
hungry kids?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have not found a single principal who will not provide lunch
for a child who is actually hungry.

Economy—Reports
3. DAVID BENNETT ( National—Hamilton East)  on behalf of ALASTAIR
SCOTT (National—Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance : What recent reports has
he received on whether recent economic growth is creating capacity and inflation
pressures within the economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Treasury’s latest monthly report
notes that although the economy is growing near capacity, inflation i s running below
expected levels. This can be partly explained by falling prices in the tradable sector, due
to a strong New Zealand dollar and weak international inflation. They also note that the
housing market is cooling. Increases in house prices are sl owing, with the annual
increase in the year to September down to 4.1 percent and the number of sales lower
than a year ago. All of this indicates that cost of living increases will remain in check
while the economy continues to grow and support more jobs and higher incomes.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How is the current low inflation environment, combined with
continued high levels of business and consumer confidence, influencing the outlook for
employment and investment?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLI SH
items.text: Positively. We have reported today that the unemployment
rate fell to 5.4 percent in September, down from 5.6 percent in June. There were 18,000
more people employed in the September quarter, and the labour force participation
rate—that is, the number of people available for work, which is already at historical
highs, and higher than most other countries in the developed world —actually increased
fractionally to 69 percent. Statistics New Zealand noted that rising employment is more
than keeping up with growing population, at a time when the population is growing at a
record level. Although business and consumer confidence have come off their highs,
they remain at elevated levels. There are strong employment intentions among
businesses. For example, the quarterly survey of the New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research reported that a net 18 percent of firms expect to increase staff numbers, and
the ANZ job advertisement series shows that job ads are at their highest levels since
2006. All of this is promi sing for more new jobs, in addition to the decreasing
unemployment rate we have seen today.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: How does the Minister expect the current positive economic outlook
will benefit New Zealand households and families?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It has always been the Government’s view that the figures
from month to month or quarter to quarter are not that important. What matters is the
longer-term trend. We have an opportunity to lock in sustainable growth, with relatively
low interest rates and relatively low inflation, at a time when the economy continues to
grow. In its pre -election fiscal update, Treasury forecast around 150,000 extra jobs by
mid-2018. It also predicted the annual average wage to increase by around $6,600 t o
$62,000 over that period. This will have a positive impact for households if cost of
living increases remain low and we can continue to support good conditions for best
business investment and new jobs. All of this will help household budgets.

5. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Is his
Government committed to evidence-based policy-making?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.
640 Oral Questions 05 Nov 2014

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, if that is the case, why does his Government not
demonstrate its commitment to evidence -based policy -making by collecting
comprehensive information on the extent of foreign ownership of New Zealand land and
housing? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has the right to ask the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY

muffled—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters

why does his Government not demonstrate its commitment to evidence -based policy-
making by collecting comprehensive information on the extent of foreign ownership of

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, we do collect information. We collect it through both
the Inland Revenue Department, which has a register of foreigners who are required to

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How can the Government be collecting “quite a lot of
information” when in the answer nothing referred to housing whatsoever, and why does
the Government not have a proper house and land register, like other countries have?

an Inland Revenue Department tax return because they own a rental property in New
Zealand, that is a house.

items.text: Does the Prime Minister not understand that that is only a
rental? What about the other forms of ownership, and what steps will the Government

foreign ownership—even though the trader over there likes it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, the Government has policies in place through the
Overseas Investment Act that we believe are set broadly in about the right place.
Although we acknowledge that t here are some foreigners who come to New Zealand
and purchase land and assets, we believe that is in the best interests of New Zealand’s
economic growth. That is why land sales to foreigners and house sales to foreigners
merrily and happily continued every single time he was on this side of the House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Not true.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, it is.

items.text: Given the Chinese Government’s priority—[Interruption]

items.text: Given the Chinese Government’s priority and crackdown
on corruption, what precautions is his Government making to en sure the proceeds of
corruption from that country do not go into New Zealand land and housing?

items.text: Well, the Overseas Investment Office goes through a thorough
process when it assesses the merits of a purchaser, but we are no t responsible for any
illegal activity that might take place in another country.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why does the Government consider that selling even more
of New Zealand’s productive capacity to foreigners is a path to prosperity?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, that is because if one looks at the history of foreign
investment in New Zealand, we can point to many examples, actually, where foreign
investment in New Zealand in even land has been very important for New Zeal and.
Take the wine industry. We all know that the member has quite an interest in the racing
05 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 641
industry. Well, the racing sector has quite a lot of investment from overseas, and last

Pharmac—Subsidised Medicines and Medical Devices
6. BARBARA KURIGER (National—Taranaki - King Country) to the Minister
of Health: Has he received any reports on access to medicines?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Yes. Pharmac’s annual
report was tabled on 4 November. It shows that last year the Pharmaceutical
Management Agency funded 26 new medicines and widened access to a further 35,
benefiting an estimated 42 ,885 additional patients in that year. This is part of the $795
million that Pharmac spent on medicines for New Zealanders last year.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: How has Pharmac helped address the costs of health care in New
Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: In its first year of managing the nationally
consistent list of hospital medicines, Pharmac has secured savings to district health
board hospitals of $3.65 million. I am advised that that figure is expected to double in
the coming year. Moreover, I am advised that as of 1 November 2014 Pharmac’s
medical devices programme has listed more than 5,000 possible medical devices across
a range of categories, including wound care, laparoscopy, and interventional cardiology.
This activity will deliver savings to district health boards worth a minimum of $9.7
million over 5 years.
State and Social Housing—Housing Stock and Initiatives
7. PHIL TWYFORD (Labour —Te Atatū)  to the Minister for Social Housing :
Does she agree with the Dominion Post that “The Government’s social -housing plan is
unclear not only in its details but in its fundamental aims,”; if not, what are the
Government’s plans and fundamental aims?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the  Minister for

items.speaker: Social Housing
items.text: No, I disagree with it. Our aims are, first, to make it easier for more
people to get into social housing;  secondly, to provide a better pipeline that enables
them to move on from social housing when they cease to need it; and, thirdly, to ensure
that the Government’s large landholdings in our metropolitan areas can contribute to the
longer-term problem of lim ited supply of affordable housing for all New Zealanders,
not just those who need social housing.
642 Oral Questions 05 Nov 2014

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Who is correct on how many they will sell: Bill English and Nick
Smith, when they have talked about up to 20 percent of the stock—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: We said that a year ago.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: —John Key—are you missing me, Nick?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: We said that a year ago.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: I will get back to you. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is not helpful for interjections to come from my right-hand
side as Mr Twyford is asking his question. He can start his question again.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Thank you. Who is correct on how many they  will sell: Bill English
and Nick Smith, when they have talked about up to 20 percent of the stock; John Key,
when he said: “less than the numbers that have been bandied around,”; herself, when
she said it could be thousands; or David Zussman, from the Mon te Cecilia Housing
Trust, who says: “ We’re told 25 percent seems on the high side and the next breath it ’s
‘a few houses ’ or is it a thousand or thousands? We’ ve no idea … There’s too many
gaps, too many guesses.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The m ember will just have to wait and see, because, as we
have all pointed out, the Government is yet to make decisions about that particular
number. But that is going to be much less important than the other number, which will
be the number of income -related rent subsidies available, and they will be increasing.
So, for instance, if we want to house 1,000 extra people under Labour’s model, it costs
roughly half a billion and takes 5 years, because you have got to build the State houses.
Under our model it will cost around $12 million to $14 million, and if the houses are
available, we can do it within a matter of months. So the number of income -related rent
subsidies available will matter more than the number of houses owned by the
Government.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Who is correct on whether the money will be reinvested in social
housing: Bill English, when he said: “there’s not much point in rebuilding stock with it
… it could go into the consolidated account.”; Bill English, when he said: “Certainly for
the foreseeable future as much as we can.”; or John Key, when he said: “The better
question to ask is: ‘Will it be used to develop new social housing?’, and the answer to
that is ‘maybe’.”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the member has pointed out, there are a lot of
opportunities to use any money from sales, but I would say to the member that the most
important piece of money is going to be what is available to provide for more people in
serious housing need. I know that Labour is having trouble und erstanding this, but it
will no longer be dictated by the number of State houses owned by the Government. We
will be able to determine, independently of the number of State houses owned by the
Government, how many people we are willing to assist. And, of c ourse, any money we
can apply from the sale of State houses to housing affordability and social housing
improvement, we will.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Does she agree with the Prime Minister that the Government’s social
housing reforms will not amount t o subsidising private landlords because “the only
people who can get income -related rents are community housing providers or Housing
New Zealand.”; if so, why has the social housing unit left the criteria open to for -profit
community housing providers and for community housing providers to utilise private
landlords rather than owning their own social houses?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Housing New Zealand does it now.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, as the former Minister of Housing said , Housing New
Zealand Corporation does that now. It uses so -called private landlords, and, of course,
the member may not be aware, but the Government spends $1.2 billion a year on a thing
called the accommodation supplement. I do not know whether the Labou r Party knows
05 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 643
about that, but that is all paid, pretty much without exception, to private landlords. I
know that the Labour Party is against that, but I can tell you that the 300,000 families
who receive it are somewhat in support of it.
Schools—Internet Access
8. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister of Education : What recent
announcements has the Government made about improving internet access in schools?
Hon NIKKI KAYE (Associate Minister of Education)  on behalf of the  Minister
of Education: This morning the Government announced $5.4 million of new funding to
enable access to upgrades for improved wireless connectivity fo r more than 400
schools. Many of these are small schools and the investment will be a significant boost
for students and teachers. These schools  will now have access to better -quality
connections and more flexible learning environments. This retrofitting o f 400 schools is
another investment on top of the $700 million already provided by this National -led
Government to enable fast, reliable internet connections to improve learning.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: Which schools will benefit from this announcement?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: The schools that will benefit are located right across New
Zealand, including Northland. From Clifton Terrace School in central Wellington,
which the Associate Minister visited this morning, to Ngataki School in Kaitaia,  the list
of schools is now available on the ministry website. The ministry will be contacting
schools across New Zealand to offer them access to this upgrade. This is another great
initiative by this National-led Government. Our Government is focused on ensuring that
New Zealand children, no matter where they live, have access to quality online learning.
Health Promotion Agency Board—Potential Conflict of Interest
9. KEVIN HAGUE (Green)  to the Minister of Health : Has he asked Health
Promotion Agency Board member Katherine Rich whether she ever used the services of
public relations adviser Carrick Graham to write attacks on public health advocates and
researchers which were published on the Whale Oil blog; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No; because as the
Minister of Health I am focusing on the things that matter to New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Will he investigate the serious allegations that Katherine Rich hired
public relations adviser Carrick Graham to write attacks on public health experts, which
were published on the Whale Oil blog?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I have asked my office to have a look at the
Whale Oil blog to see whether they can find any evidence of ex or current members of
Parliament using that blog to attack others. The only document they were able to come
up with is a guest editorial dated 2 March 2013, written by one Kevin Hague MP.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Supplementary—

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I seek leave to table a guest editorial written by
Kevin Hague MP.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If it is available on a blog, it is available to all members.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: How serious would an allegation against Katherine Rich have to be
before he asked her whether it was true or not?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Look, I think it would be very serious if an ex
or current member of Parliament was using the Whale Oil blog to attack others, and that
is why I would like to table this guest editorial—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We have already been through that.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does he  agree that the important work of the Health Promotion
Agency in reducing harm to New Zealanders from tobacco, alcohol, and unhealthy
644 Oral Questions 05 Nov 2014
foods would be undermined if a board member wearing another hat were to be involved
in attacks on public health experts in these areas?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: It is always undermining when ex or current
members of Parliament use blogs to attack others, and I think we have all had enough of
dirty politics. It is not nice to have that reminder today of Mr Hague’s previous
involvement in just such a practice.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does he agree that if the allegations against Katherine Rich are true,
then this would be incompatible with her continuing to serve as a member of the board

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: What I do agree with is that it is incompatible
for Mr Hague to ask these questions, with him being the author of a guest editorial  on
the Whale Oil blog—

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The questions that I have asked
have been ones that have not been politically loaded in any way at all, and they deserve
some answers. This Minister has failed to provide any at all. Every answer has just been
a swipe at me.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I cannot accept that the questions asked have not been politically
loaded. I think that in the case of the last question asked there is a reasonable point that
the question was not addressed by the Minister. I am going to invite Kevin Hague to ask
the last question again. As for the others, I think they have been answered
satisfactorily—they have been addressed —but I will allow the member the benefit of
the doubt with regard to the last question.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does the Minister agree that if the allegations against Katherine Rich
are true, then this would be incompatible with her continuing to serve on the board of
the Health Promotion Agency?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I disagree with the assertions in his question.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Why did he wait until 23 October 2014, the date he had to
answer his first oral question on the topic in the House, to check with the chair of the
Health Promotion Agency  as to whether Katherine Rich had conducted herself as an
ethical member of the board?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Because I was too busy getting around the
health sector, focusing on the issues that matter to New Zealanders, rather than
wallowing in this trivia.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: When did he or his predecessor first have concerns raised with
them about a potential conflict of interest or allegations of misconduct by Katherine
Rich?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: As I recall , it was on 23 October, when Kevin
Hague asked the first of his 32 questions on this topic, and he has not asked a question
on anything else to do with health in this Parliament.
Pike River Mine Disaster—Re-entry and Recovery Operation
10. Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) to the Prime

items.speaker: Minister
items.text: Does he stand by his promise with regards to the families of the Pike River

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.
Hon Damien O’Connor : Is the Prime Minister aware of the report by internationa l

05 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 645
decision by Solid Energy to abandon plans to re -enter and recover the drift to the Pike

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The right honourable Prime Minister; any of those questions.

Hon Damien O’Connor : Why did the Solid Energy representative who was in

Hon Damien O’Connor : Has the Prime Minister received a briefing from Solid

Border Control, SmartGate System—Passengers Processed and Eligibility
11. Dr SHANE RETI (National —Whangarei) to the Minister of Customs : What
reports has she received regarding the number of people using the border clearing
technology SmartGate?

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I receive regular updates on the
uptake of SmartGate, which the National -led Government introduced in 2009, and I am
very pleased to report that 10 million people have now used the technology. We have a
new 1 -week record of  76,000 people, which was set last week, and we are rapidly
approaching the record of 1 million people every 3 months. SmartGate is making a great
contribution to Better Public Services, and it is allowing the Customs Service to deploy
its officers where they are needed most.

items.speaker: Dr Shane Reti
items.text: What is the Government doing to further improve border processing
for travellers?

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Four nationalities can currently use SmartGate, and I am
hoping to announce a fifth b efore Christmas. Over time, more countries will be able to
use the technology. Recently, the age of eligibility was lowered from 16 years to 12
years, allowing more passengers to use SmartGate. The Customs Service is
investigating options for further gates and a new-generation technology, which has been
trialled successfully.
Climate Change Policy—Government Position
12. MEKA WHAITIRI (Labour —Ikaroa-Rāwhiti) to the Minister for Climate

items.speaker: Change Issues
items.text: Does he stand by his statement on the Intergovernmental Panel on
Climate Change’s 2014 report “We will use the findings from these reports to help
develop policies and to take action to mitigate our greenhouse gas emissions and to
adapt to the effects of climate change”?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.role: Acting Minister for Climate Change Issues
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: What action will he  take to realise the findings of the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that the world will need to nearly totally
phase out fossil fuel use by 2100?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: We are taking many actions. Of course, we are one of the
only countries outside the EU to have a comprehensive emissions trading scheme. Then
there is a broader range of complementary measures designed to reduce our emissions
646 Oral Questions 05 Nov 2014
and also to adapt to climate change. I would be happy to go through many of those
measures, but it would take some time.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: Based on that reply, what will he do to prevent New Zealand’s
climate-friendly businesses continuing to close or relocate overseas, like LanzaTech or
the numerous biofuel companies that left whe n his Government repealed the biofuels
obligation?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I am glad the member asked because, as announced earlier
this week, I am delighted about a renewables initiative in Southland, about other
initiatives in other parts of the country, including heavy -vehicle fuel initiatives that the
Government through the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority has been
sponsoring. Of course, there is a wide array of other things going on, like a solar firm
that has been helped by our Government to export solar into Pacific Island nations as
part of a $100 million programme exporting renewables around the Pacific that we have
put in place.

items.speaker: Meka Whaitiri
items.text: How can New Zealanders have confidence his Government will
take action to implement policies that will seriously tackle climate change when it has
weakened the emissions trading scheme twice since taking Government, refused to
restrict the flood of international carbon units, and repealed the restriction on new fossi l
fuel - powered electricity generation?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I disagree with the member. Take the electricity example
for a start —we are now at 79 percent renewables for the year to date in our electricity
system. That is the highest in a very, very long time, making us well on target to reach
our 90 percent goal by 2025. In relation to the emissions trading scheme, of course we
have done a number of things recently to make it a very workable system, including
transitioning the emissions trading scheme to effectively a domestic -only scheme from
May 2015. In May this year, of course, we closed an arbitrage loophole that threatened
the integrity of the emissions trading scheme.
Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment
Bill—Purpose and Amendment
1. POTO WILLIAMS (Labour—Christchurch East) to the Member in charge of
the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid L eave)

items.speaker: Amendment Bill
items.text: Why did she draft the Parental Leave and Employment Protection
(Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill?
SUE MORONEY (Member in charge of the Parental Leave and Employment
Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill): I drafted the bill in response
to research and evidence showing that bonding and attachment between a parent and
baby in the early months improved that child’s life outcomes, that supporting
breastfeeding to 26 weeks improved that c hild’s health, and that supporting women to
retain their connection to paid work increased their economic independence and
workplace productivity. Work subsequently undertaken by the Government
Administration Committee confirmed that extending paid parenta l leave to 26 weeks is
a cost-efficient way to promote great outcomes for families and New Zealand society.

items.speaker: Poto Williams
items.text: Are you planning any other amendments?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is a marginal question, but I will let it go. [ Interruption] Order! It
relates to the bill. Bringing the Speaker into the question was not useful. I am going to
allow the member to answer it.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Despite the sound social and economic arguments for 26 weeks’
paid parental leave for all in its current form, the bill will be defeated by National, so I
am proposing an amendment that I expect all parties can support. It extends paid
05 Nov 2014 Oral Questions 647
parental leave to 26 weeks for parents of newborn twins or triplets, parents of babies
born prematurely, o r parents of babies born with a disability. These parents face the
greatest financial pressures to return to work before it may be in the best interests of
their families to do so. My new proposal reduces the cost to just $6 million in the next
financial year.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I move, That the House
take note of miscellaneous business . What a great time to be a member of the National -
led Government —back in Parlia ment for a third term with Prime Minister John Key
showing strong leadership on the matters that make the most difference to New
Zealand. Strong leadership was today demonstrated on security matters. Strong
leadership on the economy, on health, on law and order, and on education. It was what
New Zealanders voted for, and they are going to get it in spades this term.
Meanwhile, on the other side of the House you have got this gaggle of unemployable
ne’er-do-wells. If any one of them could get a job, I am su re they would not be here.
They have not mounted one single successful attack on the Government in 4 weeks. Can
anyone remember one question that we have been asked by that crowd—

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Kevin Hague.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: —apart from Kevin Hague’s question? None at
all. They are totally lost because they are immersed in a re -run of “ Labour Survivor
2013”. You will remember that series from last year. Well, the one good guy in that got
voted on to the island by us, one of them got voted out of the caucus by them, and then I
think there is one left. Grant Robertson was skipping merrily down the aisle with
political girlfriend Jacinda Ardern, seeing the victory tape in sight, when out of the blue
came Andrew Little, the angry man from Taranaki, just fresh from increasing Jonathan
Young’s majority to record levels twice in a row. He now thinks he is the man to the
lead the Labour Party to victory. Then, of course, you have got Nanaia Mahuta
providing the light-hearted comedy moments in the background. It is all bad over there.
Then you turn to the other side there. You have got the Green Party. Well, you have
seen what those members are making in terms of a contribution to the House. Kevin
Hague—32 questions on  Katherine Rich; none on any health matters that make a
difference to New Zealanders. The only thing the Green Party has done in health is
suggest that we send homeopaths to West Africa to cure Ebola. Those people are off the
planet and completely bonkers, and the people of New Zealand notice it. Meanwhile, we
are getting on with the job.
I can tell you that with my new responsibilities as Minister of Health, it has been
very interesting going around those 20 district health boards. This is fundamentally a
different health system from when Mrs King was running it. When Mrs King was in
charge, they had patients lying on trolleys under harsh fluorescent lighting for 24 hours
without getting their operations and without getting their treatment. Mrs King was
sending patients to Australia for cancer care. Under Mrs King and then the man from
Dunedin, Mr Hodgson, they were kicking people off waiting lists. But the one thing I
can tell you about Mrs King is watch where she is sitting, because she is always sitting
beside the leader in waiting. If you look way back to when they rolled Mike Moore, she
was there. When they had the barbecue at Phil Goff’s house, she was there. When they
put Shearer in, she was there. She was there with Phil Goff, as well. So I am very
interested to see who she is going to be backing, because where Annette King goes, that
is where the Labour leadership ends up.
But what I can also tell you about the health system is you go around the doctors, the
nurses, and the lab technicians, and they  are energised. They are up for the challenge.
648 General Debate 05 Nov 2014
They are thrilled that we are delivering 44,000 extra operations every year. They are
thrilled that actually we have set those health targets. Under Labour there were no
targets; there were just strategies for Africa. No one was doing anything. All the doctors
were going to Australia. No one was getting their operations. Under us, we have raised
the immunisation rates. We are tackling rheumatic fever. We are really focusing on
those matters that make a difference to access to quality health care for New Zealanders,
and it is working. The morbidity and mortality statistics are improving. We are getting
more care out into primary care. We are actually doing a great job in improving our
children’s health. We go around our electorates and people are telling us they are happy
with the health system. My predecessor did an excellent job, but we are going to build
on that.
In this election just gone, we put another $50 million into joint and bone pain. We
are going to b e rolling out free GP visits for under -13s. That is a massive achievement.
It cuts the ground out from under Labour. Labour will never match that. People are
saying: “Look, we used to vote for Labour, but you guys understand what we’re on
about. We want our kids to be able to get the care they need. We want our kids to be in
decent schools where we get decent reporting on how they’re doing. We want to know
the streets are safe.” There is record low crime —the lowest since 1978. And do you
know what we heard yesterday? Unemployment is down to 5.4 percent. This is a
National Government delivering for New Zealanders. It is all good.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: What a riveting speech from the ciga r-
smoking Minister of Health from Northcote, the greatest friend this Parliament has ever
delivered to the tobacco industry. In fact, I am worried on behalf of Jonathan Coleman
about where he is going to get his supply of cigars now that the National Party  has
recruited half of the New Zealand tobacco industry into this Parliament. I am worried
that his supply of free cigars is about to dry up.
I want to talk about National’s great State house sell -off because this has been an
utter shambles for the last 4 weeks. It is a shambles. Let me count the ways that the
Government’s social housing policy has been a shambles. First, how many State houses
does National intend to sell off? How many? John Key said: “Well, a few State houses.”
Paula Bennett told Patrick G ower, when he asked whether it was as many as 22,000:
“Logically, maybe.” She said: “Well, it could be thousands.” Rawdon Christie asked

items.speaker: John Key
items.text: “Is 20,000 homes an accurate figure?”. John Key said: “I don’t think so, no.”
Well, the other big question t hat New Zealanders are wondering about is where will
the money be invested, the billions of dollars that will be generated from the sale of
State homes? Bill English said: “Well, um, we’re not going to rebuild houses with it. It
could go into the consolidated account.” On another occasion he said: “Well, if we want
less housing stock there is no point in rebuilding houses with it.” Will the homes be sold
to private landlords? Well, Bill English said: “We could sell them to anybody.” Bill

items.speaker: English said
items.text: “We’l l just go to the market and see who turns up, basically. Generally,
financiers and developers are not interested in social housing because it is too hard.
What drives their interest is wanting to do a better job with tenants.” So it is a shambles.
They are looking at privatising up to a third of an $18 billion public asset that has been
putting a roof over the heads of vulnerable Kiwi families for 80 years now. I think New
Zealanders deserve a bit more clarity.
But what is clear behind the bland Crosby/Tex tor assurances that trip so easily from
the tongue of Paula Bennett —“wraparound services”, “We’re working with the
community.”, “We’re all about the people.” —is that nothing could be further from the
truth. What is clear here is that Bill English has had a  back to the 1990s moment. He
and Treasury are on an ideological crusade to end State housing as we know it. Bill
English’s answer to the housing crisis, his answer to a shortage of affordable housing, is
05 Nov 2014 General Debate 649
to blame the councils, blame the Resource Managemen t Act, and flog off what State
houses the Government does own. He has basically said to the New Zealand Herald that
he just wants to get the $18 billion State housing asset off the Crown’s balance sheet.
He wants to get the Government out of the business o f actually owning houses, and
simply pay a subsidy to landlords.
There are three reasons why this is a really dumb idea. First, shifting tens of
thousands of New Zealand families out of State housing and into a voucher system, as
Paula Bennett describes i t—effectively putting money directly into the pockets of
landlords—will undoubtedly drive up rents. You do not increase supply but you fuel
demand by pumping subsidies in, just as National announced before the election, by
subsiding first -home buyers in an  overheated market. It will drive rents up. Second,
social housing tenants, under this system, will inevitably end up competing with first -
home buyers and other renters, making an already difficult housing market much worse.
The third reason is that owning  houses and having them earmarked for the express
purpose of social housing means that even when the market gets tight, as it is now, at
least you can be sure that there is a pool of housing there for the people who need it
most. Under Paula Bennett’s vouc her system, you do not get that kind of security. If
private landlords and profit providers are in the mix, as Bill English has said they will
be, they will naturally go to where the best profits can be made.
There is some kind of bizarre determination by  this Government to somehow build
an artificial market in social housing. But the market has never ever delivered
affordable, decent housing to the people who need it most.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It is always a
pleasure following the member Phil Stoner Twyford, although I must say I get
disappointed with him. I thought he was one of the nice guys, but to hear the ad
hominem attacks from t hat member, and having a series of Opposition questioners on
the other side asking questions about personalities rather than policies, shows parties in
this Parliament are bereft of ideas. Well, that is not the case on this side of the House.
I do want to say this, though.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Don’t forget, Simon, you’ve been told to be nice, not arrogant and
conceited.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: That is right. I do want to say this, though. Today it is a
privilege to speak, a day when we have had a serious debate and a series of speeches on
a very significant set of issues for New Zealand and the world. Of course, I think we can
all agree that the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL) is a barbarous organisation
that is having its  effect in the Middle East and in Islamic countries but also in Western
countries, including New Zealand. We are not immune, and we know —the Prime
Minister gave a speech today on this matter —that ISIL has been successfully recruiting
and working in New Zealand to further its evil aims.
I just want to say, while the Hon Annette King is in the House, that I agree with her
and what I thought was a very good speech from the Opposition there. She is absolutely
right. This is a question of balance. It is a quest ion of acting calmly and proportionally,
and that is exactly what the Prime Minister and this National -led Government have
done. We have not overreacted. We do, of course, have a duty of responsibility to New
Zealanders, and that is why we are making proportionate law changes that will be in this
House a little later this year —discreet legal changes to protect New Zealanders in a
proportionate way.
We are also, then, acting internationally. The only other speech I have given so far in
this House since the election was on the day after we had been elected to the United
Nations Security Council, and I was actually really proud. The flag debate was kick ing
off and I was really proud to be part of a Government, part of a country, that is outward-
650 General Debate 05 Nov 2014
looking, that is confident, and that is a responsible global corporate citizen in this world
that we live in. The quid pro quo of that, of course, is that on occa sions like this we
have to step up and act in the interests of New Zealanders, and also be good global
corporate citizens.
Because the question was asked in the House today, I also want to talk about another
serious issue facing this world of ours —climate change. I want to say quite clearly to
the member that this is a party, this is a Government, that has a strategy and a plan, and
it is working hard on what is a serious issue in this country. We have a comprehensive
emissions trading scheme. We accept —we all accept —that it is at a low price at the
moment because of global conditions, but there is a broad range of actions and
initiatives that this Government is taking to deal with this issue, not least in the
portfolios I am privileged to hold. The point I  really make to the members is that
climate change is about much more —and climate change policy is about much more —
than a price signal in the emissions trading scheme. That is why, if we go through the
things we are doing and we look at where the emissions are, 47 or 48 percent—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: The price of carbon matters.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: —Phil Stoner Twyford —come from agriculture. That is
an area where it is disruptive technology that will make the difference, and that i s why
we in this country lead the Global Research Alliance on agricultural emissions, to find a
step change in that area.
The rest of the emissions —nearly half of them —come from energy. That is why in
the area of transport, where I am Minister, we are doi ng a lot of thinking about what we
can do with our fleet and electric vehicles in some of these issues. That is why we have
got a Heavy Vehicle Fuel Efficiency programme being rolled out, which is making a
difference. That is why we have increased that pro gramme. That is also why, in the
energy sector, we make sure that our policies —and this is a perverse thing about the
left; their policies would actually set this back —are increasing renewables in this
country year on year, and, why, to the year to date, w e have 79 percent of renewables
from our electricity system. We are third or fourth at the moment in the world and we
will make 90 percent by 2025. I think that is something we should be very proud of.
We have rolled out a number of other initiatives in t hat wider energy area —[Bell
rung]—such as the renewable heat hub that I have been talking about—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just to remind
members in the general debate that the bell goes after 5 minutes and they sit down.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : In this year’s election, only one party addressed
the widespread concerns that New Zealanders have with the current i mmigration policy,
and that was New Zealand First. New Zealand First will be making immigration a major
theme of our role in this parliamentary term, too, and we will probably be the only party
to do so. This Government has a completely irresponsible and i rrational immigration
policy that is causing great damage to the interests of New Zealand. The Government
has been boasting of net immigration at uncontrolled, record levels. It is actually telling
the public that uncontrolled, record net immigration is some kind of measure of success.
It claims that this massive, unplanned immigration is an achievement. In fact, the record
numbers of migrants show that New Zealand has a slack, uncontrolled immigration
policy—in effect, an open-door policy. The numbers of migrants are nothing short of an
indictment on this Government’s incompetence on immigration.
For a start, what record numbers of immigrants show is that no consideration is given
to the relationship between immigration and housing policy, while every day brings new
horror stories about the housing crisis, especially in Auckland and Christchurch. In
Auckland, there are soaring house prices as desperate people scramble to get a home.
Hundreds of families are left to squat in caravans and garages. The Governm ent is full
05 Nov 2014 General Debate 651
of empty rhetoric about the housing crisis. Its failure to address the crisis for over 6
years continues. This Government does not have any genuine concern about the
desperate housing situation faced by thousands of New Zealanders, because the one
meaningful action it could take today, if it was serious about housing, would be to turn
off the tap to new migrants.
Of course we cannot stop New Zealanders returning to New Zealand, and neither
would we want to, but we do not have to let the rest of  the world in. All the
Government’s talk about housing is bogus. It is a total smokescreen. It is looking at only
one side of the supply and demand equation for housing because it stupidly refuses to
deal with the demand for housing generated by high immig ration. Cut immigration
now—that is what we say. That is the quickest and most effective way to relieve
pressure on the housing market immediately. It is utterly astonishing, if not bizarre, that
the Government cannot make the connection between immigration and housing.
But the Government’s immigration policy is deeply flawed for a whole range of
reasons, not just housing. Take jobs. We have over 140,000 unemployed. Tens of
thousands more have given up on finding any sort of job at all. Yet migrants are
flooding in on a temporary work visa basis. The wages and conditions of most New
Zealanders are hardly moving, leaving tens of thousands of families in severe financial
stress, and it is no wonder. Massive immigration is undermining the pay of ordinary
New Zealanders.
The truth is that the Government is only too happy to see that happening. Cheap
labour is what its corporate cronies want and it fits with National’s commitment to
globalisation. And then there is the foreign student visa racket, and a racket i t is. Why
are we allowing foreign students to work in New Zealand? In case the Government has
not noticed, there are thousands of very able young New Zealand school -leavers and
graduates who cannot find a job. Why should they have to compete with hordes of
foreign students? It does not make sense. Of course, if New Zealanders are displaced in
the job market, they may well end up on the unemployment benefit.
Thanks to wildly excessive immigration, New Zealand now has one of the fastest -
growing populations i n the OECD. That is causing great stress on housing, the labour
market, and our infrastructure generally, and there is no follow -up to see just how well
these migrants have settled in New Zealand. What checking is being done to ensure
migrants have not bec ome a burden on the taxpayer? We certainly have a lot more taxi
drivers, and some on benefits, so just what skills are we actually getting? There is no
genuine attempt to really verify that at all. This is now an open -door land. [Bell rung] It
is the usual—

member I have had to remind and the third member who has breached the rule. When
