items.speaker: JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Today has been a very important day
for New Zealand. The Prime Minister has made an announcement that I think should
give people cause to think about what dangers New Zealand actually has, particularly in
terms of our security around people who might see themselves as wanting to go off to
Syria, Iraq, and other places like that to become jihadists or terrorist fighters. We have
seen acts of terrorism in countries such as Australia and Canada. The UK has become
well used to being the subject of terrorism. The United States, many other countri es like
Indonesia, and, obviously, Syria and Iraq have had tremendous terrorism.
Terrorism is something where there is normally a public display that is there for large
audiences. It is now put on YouTube and it is used to create a sense of fear amongst as
many people as possible. It is actually, after this announcement, that we as a country
652 General Debate 05 Nov 2014
need to react to that, and the best way for us to do that is not to go immigrant -bashing
and not to revert to religious bigotry, but to remember that terrorism comes in  all forms,
and at the moment there is this one called Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. It is one
that is absolutely dedicated to the most extreme acts of violence against people such as
aid workers, and truckdrivers who give up their jobs to go to he lp deliver food in places
like Syria. That is the level of the people who are having those people’s heads cut off
with knives, videoing it, and then distributing the images around the world. Those are
the sorts of people whom we are talking about.
So toda y, when I heard the Green Party’s contribution from Metiria Turei, I, like
many other people in this House, wondered what planet she was on. I thought: “A
family group conference isn’t going to help this one.” Appeasement never really does
when you are dea ling with people who do not want to have a solution. But I did agree
with her on a couple of points. The first is the right to free speech. It is not one that I
have always seen the Greens exercise in practice, but I certainly agreed with her right to
say whatever she wanted to say today. But the other thing that I did agree with her on —
and I think it is really important —is that brute force alone does not solve this problem.
Also, however, I think it is very foolish to think that this is just an isolated gr oup of
disenchanted people who want to be made important. I think about someone like the
late—thankfully—Osama bin Laden. He was hardly a disenfranchised poor person from
Saudi Arabia, but the son of a multibillionaire. These are the sorts of people who ha ve
funded terrorism and they still do now, and there are Governments, I am sure, that are
involved in that.
It is really important, though, that we look at these changes that the Prime Minister
has discussed today and that we consider them carefully. I th ought the Labour Party,
under Annette King’s leadership, had a very sensible response. I would not suggest for a
moment—because I quite like her —that she should put her hand forward to be the next
leader of the Labour Party, but I do think it was a very re asonable and sensible
response, and certainly significantly better than the response when the Search and
Surveillance Bill came through, when the only parties that did vote for it were National,
ACT, and United Future. But, of course, all that is forgotten now, except by me.
I think it is really important, though, that we think about the fact that when we have
got 30 to 40 people, as we were told by the Prime Minister, who are of real concern to
the New Zealand SIS and that there are 30 to 40 other people whom it needs to check, it
is actually a significant number for a country like us. I would also say to those who
want to spend today attacking immigrants that most of these people, I suggest, are not
necessarily immigrants. There are quite a lot of home -grown people involved in this,
and I think many of us will have seen those who have been publicised —people who
have decided to convert to a religion in its most extreme form as an excuse for extreme
violence. That is actually what you are dealing with —not necessarily people who are
religious, but people who are violent and who want an excuse to be able to perpetrate
that violence with impunity. Those are the people whom I think we should be very
concerned about—never frightened, but concerned. We heard today about Canada and
about its Parliament being so closely aligned to ours. I mean, what terrible act was the
poor soldier guarding the war memorial doing when he was gunned down and killed —
murdered? That is what we are dealing with.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour —Māngere): Thank you for the opportunity. I do
agree with the earlier speaker that there were some serious issues debated earlier, at the
beginning of this parliamentary session. However, the public listening in to this debate
would not have known that it was serious given the way the backbenchers of the
National Party chatted, grumbled, and tried to interfere when Opposition members were
making contributions.
05 Nov 2014 General Debate 653
There is another serious matt er that I want to raise, and it has to do with the great
house sale—the State house sale by this particular Government. Only the other week I
heard Dr Shane Reti during his maiden speech make a comment that resonated with me.
He made reference to the fact that he grew up in a State house. The point that I thought
was important, and I am not sure whether the rest of the House noted it, was that he
talked about the need for us to take responsibility for those following behind us. Unlike
Dr Shane Reti, there a re members of this House who do not feel that way —who have a
similar experience, who had the advantage of being supported through a State house but
who now, in the positions they are in, do not want to pass on that support to the rest of
the population. I also heard Dr Lance O’Sullivan, another Northlander, say that when
his parents could not provide for him, his country supported him, and now, as a result of
that, he spends all of his days giving back to the community.
That is unlike what I have heard fro m the Prime Minister, who is somebody who
grew up in a State house; the Minister Paula Bennett, who grew up in a State house;
Alfred Ngaro, who, I have no doubt, grew up in a State house; and Peseta Sam Lotu -
Iiga, who grew up in a State house. It seems the y have now taken a stance that it was
OK for our country to support them, but they have taken another stance that they do not
want—[Interruption] Well, that is probably because he is named Ngaro, which is
Pukapukan for somebody who is lost, somebody who is  forgotten. He has forgotten that
the rest of New Zealand supported him, and he has now forgotten that he has a duty to
support those of us coming through who are less fortunate.
There is a waiting list of 6,000 —more than 6,000 people who are waiting to g et into
a State house because they cannot afford to pay the market rent and because they are
currently living in someone’s garage, sharing a relative’s living room, in a boarding
house, in an emergency house, or, as we saw the other day, living in a car or  in a
caravan park. These people shower at the public toilets. They use sports club facilities to
get dressed and prepare their children to go to school. They do not have regular incomes
because one week they will have a 40 -hour week, which they are paid f or, and another
week they will not have any hours because of the casualisation of the work they are in.
That is the reality. We currently have a housing crisis that this Government refuses to
acknowledge. It refuses to acknowledge that there is child pove rty. We do not hear
Government members using that particular word any more. They continue to say
something else to try to cover the situation, the crisis we are in.
Prior to the election, a young woman came to my office. Her mother had passed
away. There were three of them —she and her two young siblings. She was 18 years of
age, with a young sibling aged 6 and another one of 3 years of age. Housing New
Zealand was determined to evict them because the house was in their mother’s name.
These three young people could not live with a relative because the auntie already had a
full house. Prior to the election, we managed to convince Housing New Zealand to find
sustainable accommodation for them. After the election, guess what? Instead of giving
them the proper notice, Housing New Zealand then said that they had to move out to the
private sector. They had to find —and this is a quote from the official’s mouth —
“sustainable accommodation”. I could not convince those officials that these three
young children needed a house to live in. In fact, what they said to me was that it is
against Government policy to house this group of young people, who could not live on
their own because their parent had died. So guess what? The Government knows there
is a housing crisis, but it does not care. It does not care one iota.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak after the member

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: This is it—this is what has become of this speech.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. I think the member
will just change his tone a bit. Thank you.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: This is what has become of the speech. It is the classic speech,
the socialist speech that keeps coming out, and, by the way, the assumption that I grew
up in a State house is not true. This is the thing —all these assumptions about who we
are as Polynesian people growing up, the assumptions in his speech that talked about the
knight coming in to save our communities, and save our people. In other words, they
cannot save themselves. Well, this is what happens. Labour Party members keep saying:
“We are here, as the Labour Party, to save you.” Well, guess what? Here is some
news—our community does not need you to save it. Why? Because we can save
ourselves. That is right. But this is what has happened —those sorts of speeches have
become a one-trick pony. It is the same thing over and over again , hence the reason that
over a mil lion New Zealand ers did not vote for the Labour Party. Labour has had the
poorest result in the history of the Labour Party —in 92 years. So it is going to have to
take some lessons from that.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Not as bad as the National Party in 2002. Don’t forget that.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: You can shout all you like, but here is the reason why we are
making a difference. Why? Because when we talk about poverty, hardship, and
difficulty, it is not about saying: “Here are the thing s we are going to do for you.” Our
communities do not need to be told that we are here to save them. All they want and all
they need is opportunity and a fair go. So here is the reality.
Out there in west Auckland, in Te Atatū, where I went and campaigned  for 2½
months, here is the difference it made. In 2½ months the people of Te Atatū turned
round and said they halved the majority for a Labour seat that had been Labour for some
time.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Turned around and said they wanted P hil Twyford, not Alfred
Ngaro.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: That is right. The majority of the party vote was increased from
700 in 2011 to nearly 2,000. That is what actually happened in 2½ months. Here is a
telling sign. When I was at Rutherford College,  Will Flavell came out and said this to
me: “Geez, you’re going hard, aren’t you?”. I asked him how long he had been out in
the west and he said: “Maybe some 10 years.” So here is a lesson from the wise about
how it rolls out in the west. You either go hard or you go home.
Our communities want to hear the messages that make a difference, so you talk about
housing and how that makes a difference. Our communities heard about KiwiBuild —
100,000 homes, 10,000 per year —but here is the telling thing in the debate . Down at
McLaren Park, when Phil Stoner Twyford was asked this question: “So you’re saying
you’ve got 10,000 per year?”, he said that was correct. But on Q+A on Sunday he said
he could build 400 in the first year, 8,000 in the second, and 12,000 in the ne xt. That is
right—it is accumulative over a period of time. People began to see through the lies and
realised that is not what makes a difference. Our housing policies are making a
difference.
Here is the other thing. The issues around a capital gains tax  did not make a
difference. That is right. [ Interruption] Wahine, you can keep talking and crying all the
time—here is what made a difference. All of a sudden it was a failed policy. You no
longer talk about it. Why? Because it became an inheritance tax.
The ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Hon Trevor Mallard: Order!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: So here is the thing that becomes important. Time and time
again our communities are saying that the policies are weak, the implement ation does
05 Nov 2014 General Debate 655
not happen, and the reality is there is nothing new. You are going to have to change
your message because it is not getting through.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni

appropriate for that member to say that you need to change.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Yes, and if the member had
been listening she would have heard me correct him at the time.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Here is the other bit in the issues around poverty that we
believe is making a difference. Just this afternoon, for instance, we were down here
looking at the Big Picture art exhibition. Over there the young children from
Pukehamoamoa School had won the p rize, and why? Because they showed a picture
that showed that poverty is a very complex issue in our communities. We know that
there is hardship in our communities. We know that there are difficulties. So how are
we solving this? We are dealing with the is sues in hardship, for instance, with free GP
visits for children under 13, ensuring that they get access to health services that are
there. What are we also doing, for instance? We are ensuring that we are engaging into
communities so that they enrol into early childhood education. We know the difference
that that makes to our communities —and it is making a difference. We know how that
is engaging our communities as well.
I also want to talk about the fact that our Pasifika communities are changing and
moving towards a value -based, National -led Government and the things that we are
doing. We are seeing it happen constantly, over and over again. Why? Because those
values of opportunity are constantly coming through for our people as well. Here is the
difference that we know that it is making. The economy is growing by 3.9 percent.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: At last. Health promotion is the discipline of improving
health by addressing not only the individual factors  that drive illness but also the risk
environments that drive illness. Health promotion involves going beyond education and
social marketing and trying to address and change those environments. Health
promotion funding over the past 6 years has more than h alved. That is one of the
reasons why we supported the creation of the Health Promotion Agency. We felt it
could make a difference. But our eyebrows were certainly raised —and those of many
health promoters were raised—by the appointment of Katherine Rich to the board of the
Health Promotion Agency. That is because Mrs Rich appears to have a pretty deep
conflict of interest and it was very hard to see how that was going to be managed. The
main causes of preventable illness and death in this country are tobac co, alcohol, and
unhealthy food and drink. Mrs Rich’s day job is in fact to maximise the consumption of
and profit from those very products, which conflicts with the role that she would have
as a member of the Health Promotion Agency board to minimise the consumption of
and harm from those products. It is a fundamental conflict of interest. It was hard to see
how she was going to be able to manage it.
Managing conflicts of interest is not, as the Minister of Health would have us
believe, a trivial matter. It goes beyond an ethical duty —it is a legal duty. The Crown
Entities Act sets out specific legal duties that members of the Health Promotion Agency
board have got, and there are three levels. The first is to complete and maintain a
register of interests —professional interests, personal interests; a general register. The
second level is that when a potential conflict of interest arises in relation to a specific
agenda item that is being considered by the board, the member of the board must
declare that pote ntial conflict of interest. The third level is that in relation to that
matter—in relation to that potential conflict —the member must withdraw from
discussion and decision making in relation to that matter.
I have to say that Katherine Rich has been very diligent in her completion of that first
duty. She has maintained a register of interests, but she has completely failed in both of
656 General Debate 05 Nov 2014
those other duties. She has never ever —not even once —declared a conflict of interest
with any item being considered by the Health Promotion Agency board, and that is
despite every single meeting that she has attended including discussion by the Health
Promotion Agency of strategy on at least one of, and usually more, alcohol, toba cco, or
food and drink. She has failed in that legal duty. She has never ever —not even once—
withdrawn from any discussion of or decision making in relation to any matter being
considered by the board. She has failed absolutely to meet her ethical and legal
obligations. That is not just some technical or theoretical duty that she has slipped up
on; it is a fundamental thing.
So, for example, the Health Promotion Agency has submitted in favour of the
Smoke-free Environments (Tobacco Plain Packaging) Amendmen t Bill. Katherine Rich
submitted against it. Over the past several weeks, questions in this House have been
exploring the very serious allegations made against Mrs Rich in Nicky Hager’s book
Dirty Politics—that she engaged Carrick Graham to commission and write blog posts
for the Whale Oil Beef Hooked blog, attacking public health experts. I do not know
whether that allegation is correct or not. If it is not, I would be very interested to know
what the initials “KR” stand for. That is a very serious allegat ion, and what we have
heard from Minister Coleman today, and in the House over the past several weeks, is
that he has not even bothered to ask Katherine Rich whether the allegations are true. She
has not denied it in public. She has not issued a defamation  action against Nicky Hager.
The Minister has not even commenced an investigation as to whether the allegations are
true. This is a Government that has been mired by allegations of cronyism, and Minister
Coleman appears intent on continuing that.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: I felt fortunate to be given a general
debate spot today by the Hon Gerry Brownlee, especially in relation to the
announcement that was made today by the Prime Minister as to what we are planning or
looking at doing to help with the threat that the Islamic State of Iraq and Levant (ISIL)
presents not just in the Middle East but as a growing global threat. There are just a few
facts that I want to remind everyone in the House of, because I have listened to the
contributions and it is good to see that there is general support and consensus around
what our Prime Minister is doing.
Iraq is a sovereign country. I was lucky enough to be there and help to deliver the
first elections after the toppling of Saddam Hussein. It is a sovereign country. It does
have a democracy and its people have voted in a democratically elected Government.
They have asked for help because they are having a tough time of it there at the
moment. They have got a terror group that has grown and that is operating across two
borders. It is well -organised. It is well resourced. Never before have we seen these
groups have access to the types of funds that they currently have access to. The Hon
Gerry Brownlee made a very good point that they are not just operating in the Middle
East; they are operating in places like Somalia, Yemen, and Nigeria, and their tactics are
changing.
The one thing that I was very pleased and relieved to see as a member of the National
caucus was how carefully our leadership group is approaching this. I do not feel like we
could have a stronger team leading our country into this than our Prime Minister; the
Hon Gerry Brownlee, the Minister of Defence; and the Hon Murray McCully, our
Minister of Foreign Affairs,  and who is , probably at the moment in this country —in
fact, he would be in this country —the one person who has got more knowledge than
anyone in terms of what is happening globally, with the work that he has put in and the
fantastic result that he and his team delivered in our securing a seat on the United
Nations Security Council; and, of course, Chris Finlayson, the top legal mind in the
country in terms of making sure that we remain compliant.
05 Nov 2014 General Debate 657
I was lucky enough back in 2002 -03 to be responsible for overseeing the training of
the newly formed security forces inside Iraq, which included the Iraqi Police Service,
the Iraqi National Guard, the Facilities Protection Service, the border and customs
police, and the tactical support  unit. As part of that role, I oversaw the training that was
delivered by Kiwis, Brits, and also Americans. I can tell you now that it made a huge,
fundamental difference in the way that the Iraqi security services were able to deploy
and operate. So I was very pleased to hear that the Prime Minister is considering this as
an option —for us to make a contribution —because it would make a real, tangible
contribution to helping Iraq out in its struggle against ISIL.
I just want to acknowledge the Peshmerga fig hters, who are really taking the fight to
ISIL at the moment. I was lucky enough to work with them also. They are certainly a
group that are not short on courage and they are passionate about their homeland, and
they are showing that they are putting up a stiff resistance. I acknowledge the Iraqi
forces as well, which are doing the best that they can within the environment that they
have to operate in.
I will just say a little bit about that environment and some of the risks that they face.
We do not hear about it and we do not really talk about it too much, but you have to
remember—and I think the Prime Minister alluded to it today —that a big part of ho w
these terror groups operate is through kidnapping. Actually, families of members of the
armed forces are targeted. That, of course, puts them in a very difficult situation. What
would any of us do if we were faced with a situation where our family, our c hildren, or
our wife has been taken and there are demands put on you in terms of whether or not
you will actually turn up the next day and deploy with your colleagues? So this is one of
the challenges that they really face.
In terms of their tactics, I th ink David Shearer made a very good point and the Prime
Minister backed it up. We are not being alarmist. No one wants to be alarmist. Every
single night we go to bed, and probably most of us are unaware that the police are out
there dealing with all types of crimes that we will never see, that will never touch us,
but that are happening. But they are trained, and they understand how to deal with
those.

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: The big State house sell -off is
real, and it is amongst us, and it is the result of this Government and its plans to
abdicate its responsibility in the State housing space.
I want to stand and bring up a very localised situation that I am experiencin g in the
Hastings and Napier area when it comes to a real lack of State housing stock. I have got
numerous reports in the papers that go back months and months, saying that the
situation is getting worse. I am having meetings on a regular basis. It was qui te hurtful
to hear the honourable Alfred Ngaro talking about people having to look after
themselves because, I am proud to say, our first family home was achieved through the
capitalisation of my sister’s family benefit. That allowed my family —my parents a nd
five siblings —to get on the homeownership ladder. I acknowledge that and we are
proud. She keeps reminding us that she actually owns the family home, even though she
is 55 now.
But in all seriousness, there have been some great policies in the past tha t kept our
obligations as a State, as a Crown, to help those who do want to get into
homeownership. I just want to remind this House that those policies in the past did
actually work and we did get people into homeownership. I want to stand and say there
is nothing that makes you more proud than to know that you own your own home. But
the reality for a lot of the communities and constituents we on the Opposition side
represent is that just getting a decent roof over their heads for themselves and their
family is a basic right for every New Zealander.
658 General Debate 05 Nov 2014
Like I said, I want to put a spotlight on three areas. When I spoke earlier addressing
the Speech from the Throne, I highlighted some amazing people —local champions who
are working in the advocacy role of their  own will and through their own commitment
because they see the hardships many, many families are facing in the Hastings and
Napier area. I want to acknowledge them for what they do on behalf of those on the
long waiting list.
Kiri Swindell is a wonderful  lady from Napier, who every Friday at 6 p.m. is in the
Clive Square soup kitchen feeding between 15 and 40 homeless people, mainly men —
15 to 20 in Napier who come to her soup kitchen, which she provides with her husband.
She does not work for any agency. She does not receive any funding. She does it
because she sees a need. So I want to acknowledge what Kiri says. She, along with the
other advocates who I know in the Hawke’s Bay, are meeting on a regular basis so that
we can bring the issues on homelessnes s and the struggles of people in both Napier and
Hastings to the public’s attention. A lot of it is getting led by this Government, saying
that everything is kei te pai, when really we all know that at the end of it, it is not. So I
want to acknowledge Kiri and her husband for the work they do in Napier.
I want to also acknowledge Florence Karaitiana, who is another local housing
advocate who works in the Raureka, Camberley, and Flaxmere areas. These women
have taken it upon themselves to be informed about  the housing situation. Florence has
aerial photographs of all the State homes of Raureka, of Camberley, and of Flaxmere —
all the State homes. Her question is: why are they vacant when we have so many on the
waiting list? It is a pretty simply question. In fact, they were in my electorate office and
we literally counted each State home from these area maps and we got up to at least 100
in those three suburbs.
It baffles me that we hear from the Government that it has got a housing plan when
in reality, when I go back to my electorate office in Hastings and Napier, I have people
coming in daily who are waiting for State houses. It is just not fair. In Maraenui we
have over 100 vacant State homes boarded up. I want to acknowledge that we have had
some new two -bedroom, futureproofed homes built in Maraenui, but the supply is not
keeping up with the demand. Thank you.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: It is my pleasure to speak in this
general debate tonight because it is my turn to highlight the fantastic work that this John
Key - National Government is doing to enhance and strengthen our community across
New Zealand but also in Invercargill and Southland. All throughout the campaign, the
Opposition cried how rubbish New Zealand was, how terrible it was to live here, and
how the sky was falling. Well, New Zealand did not agree, and I certainly do not agree.
As such, I am extremely proud of the achievements that this Government has made
in these difficult economic times to grow our economy, to deliver better public services,
and to support our families. This is a Government that is not afraid to think outside the
box. We have initiatives novel to the Opposition, such as a Business Growth Agenda,
implementing strategies to keep New Zealand open for business, and negotiating
essential free -trade agreements, which are especially important for areas such as
Southland that have an export -driven economy. New Zealand simply does not have
enough people to  sell our wares to, and we must treat the rest of the world as our
business partners.
This Government is also investing in infrastructure. We are investing in ultra -fast
fibre to connect even our most isolated businesses with the rest of the world, and
Southland is a prime example. Even though we live at the bottom of the world and our
hair is swept with the winds off the polar ice caps, our businesses are thriving. They are
producing more, they are hiring more staff, and they are generating higher incomes  for
our people.
05 Nov 2014 General Debate 659

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Some pretty good MPs, too.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: Thank you. In fact, unemployment figures released today in the
household labour force survey say that the South Island unemployment rate is 3.4
percent. That is fantastic.
Unlike the Labour Party, this Government is a dynamic one. We are not one -trick
ponies. Not only do we care about building a strong economy but we care about our
families getting ahead too. Take health care, for example. We introduced free doctors
visits and prescriptions for children under 6, and now we are extending it to children
under 13 years of age. This means that cost is not a barrier to our children getting the
medical attention that they need and early intervention, including immunisation
programmes, to keep our kids healthy. I am so pleased that another doctor’s surgery in
Invercargill has signed up to that scheme to keep our Southland kids healthy. This year
our public health care budget will reach a record $15.6 billion.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: $15.6 billion. We are making each dol lar go further, and we are
focused on front -line results. There are more elective surgeries to reduce pain, restore
independence, and improve quality of life. Since 2008 there are 1,600 more doctors and
3,200 more nurses in district health boards. We care about New Zealanders’ health and
their lifestyles.
I want to pay tribute to the Southland Institute of Technology. Yesterday it signed a
memorandum of understanding with an Indonesian polytechnic, LP3i Polytechnic, to
develop an exchange programme not onl y to enrich, obviously, Invercargill’s cultural
diversity but to bring students over for a staircase option to allow them to study, after
they have completed their diplomas, to complete a degree in commerce, applied
management, or hotel management. This is  indicative of the standard and the quality of
the courses offered by the Southland Institu te of Technology. This John Key - National
Government has a goal of doubling the total value of international education to $5
billion by 2025, as set out in our Busi ness Growth Agenda. The polytech and
Invercargill are contributing to this through such alliances, and I look forward to
meeting the first students taking part in this exchange soon.
There is much still to be achieved, but New Zealand, Invercargill, and S outhland are
coming out of one of the worst financial crises since the Great Depression and we are
well on the way to a more prosperous and meaningful position. I look forward to being
part of this positive and pragmatic Government now and in the future.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: This Government is
embarking upon the most significant change in State and social housing that this
country has seen in 80 years. It is going  to be a disaster. It is going to be an absolute
disaster. When we look at the housing issues in this country, the spectrum of need goes
from homelessness —people living in cars, garages, and tents —right through to the
other end where only those with the mo st wealth can actually afford a home these days.
It is shameful what this Government is attempting to do to those most vulnerable, those
most in need of housing.
We are talking about State housing —our housing; housing that is owned by the New
Zealand taxpayer, housing that we are proud of, that we should be proud of, and that we
should continue to invest in. It is State housing, which this Government wants to morph
into the terminology of social housing. Let us get it right. State housing is housing that
we own as a nation. It supports our beneficiaries, supports our low -income families,
supports people who are unwell, supports young parents, supports our older people, and
supports our community organisations. When I ran a refuge, I had the privilege of
having community support through State housing to support women and children who
660 General Debate 05 Nov 2014
were trying to escape violence. That is what State housing is about. It serves people who
cannot access affordable housing through the private rental market.
Let us look at what  the Minister of Finance, Bill English, said today about the
Government’s changes to State housing —the proposed sell -off of some of the State
houses. Some of them will go to social housing providers, but not all. Some of them will
be retained by Housing Ne w Zealand, and others —the rest of them —will be sold. Who
to? To private landlords, that is who. What will they do with them? There are two
pathways of thought around this. What is the justification for selling State houses? The
Minister Bill English said t hat they needed to be fit for purpose, so they needed to be
the right type, in the right place, in the right condition, and of the right size. OK, so he is
probably talking about three-bedroom homes, which are not the right size for families in
need and for some people in need.
There are 6,000 people on the Housing New Zealand  priority A waiting list. About
1,400 to 2,000 of those people are waiting for transfers from one type of house to
another. There would be more than 4,000 —nearly 4,500 —people alone wa iting for a
type of house. There are some real difficulties that I have with reviewable tenancies,
which will move people from their current State houses and into other types of housing.
It means that we are putting vulnerable people out into the private h ousing market, and
letting them drift. We are divesting ourselves of housing, with no plans to invest that
funding back into the housing market. If the Government does have plans, tell us about
them. Where is the transparency? What are your plans? What are you going to do? What
is the Government planning to do?
My second area of concern is around the accommodation supplement. There has not
been a lot of discussion about what is going to happen around the accommodation
supplement. There has been really limi ted discussion around this. Who does the
accommodation supplement support? It supports the private landlords —the private
landlords—who are likely to pick up some of these State houses that we are selling.
Will the Government actually tell us what it is bud geting, what it is committing to in
terms of the accommodation supplement? Minister English said today that the changes
to social housing, State housing, was going to provide more money to be available for
people and their housing needs —not more housing; m ore money. This signals to me
that there is going to be more money available for private landlords for the
accommodation supplement, and that is a shame. It is a tragedy. We need to build
houses, not provide more money for private landlords—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: To put rents up.

items.speaker: POTO WILLIAMS
items.text: —to put rents up, to live off the poor, low -income folk who
actually want decent housing and deserve decent housing.
What has this Government committed to pay directly into the pockets of p rivate
landlords?
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
